title: Chad Tracy’s controversial Game 1 move backfires as Red Sox fans react
description: Red Sox manager Chad Tracy is facing criticism after his fifth-inning pitching change backfired against the Yankees. Rookie Payton Tolle had allowed one run before Tracy replaced him with Erik Miller, who surrendered a solo homer to Ben Rice. Boston’s 9-0 loss intensified questions about the decision.
fullText:
The Boston Red Sox entered their postseason opener hoping rookie Payton Tolle could challenge the New York Yankees. Instead, one fifth-inning pitching change became a major talking point after Boston suffered a shutout defeat.

Manager Chad Tracy pulled Tolle with two outs and nobody on base, choosing left-handed reliever Erik Miller to face Yankees slugger Ben Rice. Three pitches later, Rice sent a fastball over the center-field wall.

The home run gave New York a two-run advantage, and Boston ultimately lost 9-0. Although the Yankees controlled much of the game, Tracy's decision immediately drew criticism from frustrated Red Sox fans.

Tolle started Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series on Sept. 29 at Yankee Stadium. The 23-year-old rookie received the assignment after delivering encouraging performances during his first major league season.

Through four innings, Tolle had allowed one earned run on five hits while recording four strikeouts. He had also issued one walk, keeping Boston within striking distance despite facing New York's dangerous lineup.

The pivotal moment arrived in the bottom of the fifth. Tolle retired Paul Goldschmidt on one pitch for the second out, but Tracy decided to make a change with the left-handed Ben Rice approaching.

Tracy summoned Miller, another left-hander, to face Rice. The matchup appeared designed to neutralize the Yankees slugger, but the result quickly undermined the manager's decision.

Miller threw a 97-mph fastball that landed over the middle of the plate. Rice connected solidly, driving the pitch over the center-field fence for a solo home run that doubled New York's lead.

The sequence unfolded in only three pitches, turning an already scrutinized decision into an immediate talking point. Miller recorded just one out before Boston replaced him, leaving fans questioning the timing and reasoning behind the move.

Fun fact: Ted Williams remains the last MLB player to finish a season batting over .400, hitting .406 for Boston in 1941.

The home run triggered a wave of criticism on social media, with fans questioning why Tracy removed Tolle when the rookie had recorded two outs and faced nobody on base.

Some supporters argued that Tolle deserved an opportunity to finish the inning. Others focused on the decision to replace one left-handed pitcher with another, especially when Miller struggled during his final regular-season appearances.

One fan described the move as a bad decision, while another questioned why Boston would remove Tolle only to bring in a reliever who appeared less effective. The reaction reflected frustration with both timing and execution.

Tracy defended the change by pointing to the situation in the batting order. Rice had doubled earlier against Tolle, and the manager believed Miller offered a favorable opportunity to get the dangerous hitter out.

"Not necessarily just the pitch count, but you're trailing already, you're moving through the lineup for the third time," Tracy explained after the game, according to NBC Boston's report.

Tracy added that Rice had already hit a double against Tolle and that Miller presented a suitable matchup. The manager's explanation clarified his thinking, although the resulting home run intensified questions about the decision.

Tolle was not dominating every at-bat, but he had kept the Yankees' offense relatively contained. His five hits allowed and one earned run through 4⅔ innings gave Boston a chance to remain competitive.

The rookie had thrown 83 pitches when Tracy removed him. NBC Boston noted that Tolle exceeded that pitch count 20 times during the regular season, making the decision particularly noticeable to observers.

No one can know whether Tolle would have retired Rice or completed the inning successfully. However, his performance before the change gave critics a clear reason to question whether removing him was necessary at that moment.

While Boston's pitching decisions attracted attention, Yankees starter Cam Schlittler delivered the strongest performance of the night. He limited the Red Sox to two hits and one walk while striking out 10 batters over 6⅓ scoreless innings.

Schlittler's command and velocity repeatedly frustrated Boston's hitters, leaving the visitors unable to build meaningful offensive momentum. The Red Sox never scored, making it difficult to challenge New York even before the game's late innings.

The Yankees eventually won 9-0, scoring seven runs across the final two innings. That wider margin reflected Boston's broader struggles, meaning Tracy's fifth-inning decision was significant without being the only reason for the defeat.

Miller's appearance ended quickly after Rice's home run, forcing Boston to continue navigating its bullpen earlier than planned. The manager's choice also became more consequential as the game moved into its later innings.

The Red Sox struggled to contain New York after the fifth, and the Yankees extended their advantage with a powerful late offensive surge. Boston's pitching staff could not prevent the contest from becoming a lopsided defeat.

Although the game's final score magnified the scrutiny, the bullpen's overall performance and the offense's inability to score also mattered. The loss was a team result, even as Tracy's decision became its most debated managerial moment.

The 9-0 defeat left the Red Sox needing a response in Game 2 of the best-of-three Wild Card Series. Instead, New York won again and completed a two-game sweep.

Boston started veteran Sonny Gray in the second game, while the Yankees turned to left-hander Max Fried. Fried allowed 1 run over 6 innings, and New York pulled away for a 9-2 victory.

Tracy's handling of Tolle remained part of the postgame discussion, but Boston's broader problems also mattered. The Red Sox were outscored 18-2 across the series and were eliminated before reaching the Division Series.

The Red Sox lost 9-0 to the Yankees in Game 1 on Sept. 29, 2026.

Chad Tracy removed rookie starter Payton Tolle with two outs in the fifth inning.

Erik Miller replaced Tolle but gave up a solo homer to Ben Rice.

Fans criticized the timing of the pitching change and the lefty-on-lefty matchup.

Tracy said he wanted Miller to face Rice after the Yankees slugger had doubled earlier.

Boston then lost Game 2, 9-2, and was eliminated in a two-game Yankees sweep.

title: Deterministic Simulation Testing in Celld
description: How celld controls time and execution order to find bugs with deterministic simulation testing, explained through interactive diagrams, pseudocode, and a race it discovered.
fullText:
We are building celld, a runtime for Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects applications on your own machines. It can run with an S3-compatible object store as its only external service dependency.

celld is a distributed system. Making distributed systems reliable is hard, partly because we can unintentionally rely on assumptions that don’t hold in practice, even when we know the pitfalls. Peter Deutsch’s The Eight Fallacies of Distributed Computing lists eight such assumptions, including “The network is reliable” and “Latency is zero.”

A bug can depend on a particular sequence of delayed messages, failed writes, and node restarts. Those events can happen in a different order on the next test run, making the failure difficult to reproduce. We need to be able to repeat the failing run so we can investigate the cause and check whether a proposed fix really resolves the problem.

That is why we use deterministic simulation testing (DST). Our simulator is still under development and is not included in celld’s public repository, but it has already found previously unknown bugs. In this article, we’ll walk through how DST works in celld and how it helped us find, reproduce, and fix one of those bugs.

DST runs celld’s production code in an environment controlled by a simulator.

A cell in celld runs application code and has its own SQLite database. As cells do their work, celld handles events such as incoming requests, completed storage operations, and timer firings. The code that selects the next event is separate from the code that handles it. This lets the simulator control the order of events while running the same event-handling code as in production.

The simulator also controls when asynchronous tasks run and how object storage responds. It can delay a write or make it fail. It can advance simulated time without waiting for real time to pass. We use this control to test how time-dependent behavior, such as retries and alarms, interacts with other events.

We configure which requests and faults the simulator can explore. Within those limits, it uses random choices to generate requests, select what runs next, decide whether storage operations succeed or fail, and choose which faults occur and when.

A seed is the starting value for its random-number generator. With the same code, settings, and seed, we get the same sequence, intermediate states, and result. We can explore different runs by changing the seed, then repeat a failing run to trace where things went wrong.

After each action, a checker uses observed responses and stored data to test invariants: conditions we define that the system must uphold throughout a run. The test initializes celld with the simulated environment, then explores actions up to a configured limit. In pseudocode:

Here, an action is something the simulator can advance: delivering a request, letting a task run, advancing the simulated clock, or completing a storage operation. If no actions are available, the test checks its completion conditions, such as whether all planned requests have finished.

The simplified replay below starts after Cell A has inserted a row into SQLite. Watch how the data is saved to object storage before celld receives confirmation. Other requests or background tasks can run in that gap, while celld is still waiting to return success to the client. Bugs can emerge when these operations interleave in unexpected ways. The simulator controls these steps separately so we can explore different execution orders and replay those that expose a bug.

Press Next to step through choosing an action, animating it, and revealing its result.

The row is in SQLite. The client is still waiting for success.

The replay above shows a successful request. Next, we’ll look at an execution order that exposed a bug in celld.

An alarm schedules a cell to run application code at a specified time. The cell need not stay in memory until then: celld can unload an idle cell to make room for others and load it again in time to run its alarm.

The alarm's scheduled time is stored in the cell's SQLite database. If the cell has been unloaded, finding its alarm from SQLite alone would mean opening its database again. Doing that for every cell would be expensive, so celld instead scans wake entries in object storage. Each entry identifies a cell and when to reactivate it. Once the cell is active, celld reads the scheduled time from SQLite to determine when to run the alarm.

When we found this bug, celld reused wake entries to reduce the number of writes to object storage. For example, an application could delete a 10:00 alarm and then set a new one for 10:05. If the 10:00 wake entry was still present, celld could reuse it to reactivate the cell at 10:00, early enough for the new alarm. Once the cell was active, celld would read 10:05 from SQLite and wait until then to run the alarm.1

Deleting the 10:00 alarm clears its scheduled time from SQLite. Once that change has been saved to object storage, celld returns success to the client. A separate cleanup task removes the 10:00 wake entry later, so the client does not have to wait for that extra storage operation. The client can therefore set the 10:05 alarm while the old cleanup is still waiting to run.

After celld confirms that the 10:05 alarm is set, a wake entry must remain that can reactivate the cell by 10:05. The simulator checks that this remains true until the alarm runs or is canceled.

The figure below shows how this invariant is violated when the old cleanup runs after the 10:05 alarm has been set.

Cell A has a 10:00 alarm in SQLite and a 10:00 wake entry in object storage.

In this run, both deleting the 10:00 alarm and setting the new 10:05 alarm returned success while the old cleanup waited. When the simulator finally advanced that cleanup, it removed the 10:00 wake entry that the new alarm still needed. The checker reported an invariant violation: the 10:05 alarm was still set in SQLite, but no wake entry remained to reactivate the cell.

If the node restarted before 10:05, the missing wake entry could prevent the alarm from running, despite the earlier success response.

The simulator found this failing order by exploring requests and pending work. We had not written a test that prescribed this sequence.

We replayed the failure with the same code, settings, and seed. Each run let us inspect the moment the old cleanup deleted the needed wake entry, without searching for the failing order again.

Since then, we have changed the wake-entry design. Each new alarm setting gets its own entry in object storage. A delayed deletion for an older alarm can only remove that older entry, leaving the new one intact. Old entries are removed once celld has confirmed they are no longer needed.

We turned the failing run into a regression test that repeats the requests and cleanup order shown above. It checks that the new alarm keeps a usable wake entry.

The regression test checks the invariant during the run, not just at the end. If the wake entry disappeared and was later restored, checking only the final state would miss the violation.

The simulator is still under development, but it has already helped us find and fix previously unknown bugs in celld. Next, we will test more combinations of requests, storage failures, and node restarts. For example, a node could restart during a storage outage and receive new requests before storage recovers.

We will also add checks for more of celld’s guarantees. A write reported as successful, for example, must survive a node restart. When these tests find a bug, we can replay the failure, fix it, and keep the sequence as a regression test.

title: The Inner Worlds of Neon Genesis Evangelion
description: A Japanese-television phenomenon that sparked a boom in anime production and fandom, Hideaki Anno’s magnum opus is a mind-bending mix of kinetic action, sci-fi spectacle, and introspective human drama.
fullText:
“When did it start? Since when did animation stop being interesting? That is, animation itself may have stopped being interesting, and I myself may have been unable to maintain interest in animation. Both may be true. Animation may be over.”

Hideaki Anno wrote these words in 1993, just two years before he would definitively disprove them with the creation of his magnum opus, Neon Genesis Evangelion (1995–6). His pessimism was not without cause: the anime industry was in a slump, even before the bursting of Japan’s “bubble economy” in 1992 lead to major contractions. In particular, the science-fiction and mecha (a.k.a. “giant robot”) genres that had forged Anno’s own fandom, and on which he’d cut his professional teeth, had mostly disappeared from the airwaves and migrated to the home-video market. Anno and his studio Gainax had broken it big there with his first directorial project, the 1988 miniseries Gunbuster—an eccentric mash-up of giant robots, sports anime, hard sci-fi, and the then-recent Tom Cruise blockbuster Top Gun—but had hit much harder resistance on television. His first TV series, Nadia: The Secret of Blue Water (1990–1), suffered an arduous production, and left Gainax with major financial losses. Anno found himself emotionally in step with the medium he loved—which is to say, he spent the early nineties in a period of severe depression.

Produced in the wake of this personal and professional malaise, Evangelion proved both an emotional exorcism and a huge commercial paradigm shift. Its twenty-six-episode run sparked a new boom in anime production, fandom, storytelling, and merchandising that carried into the twenty-first century. It popularized the late-night anime block—where shows were broadcast in inexpensive time slots late at night or in early morning hours, creating a haven for more experimental and adult-oriented series—while further intensifying the already-hot home video market. And that was all before Evangelion left Japan: the series was also a crucial leader in establishing a durably popular anime market in the United States and other English-speaking territories. In the nineties, anime in America largely existed either as an underground, bootlegged subculture or through dubbed “cartoons” on TV edited to disguise their “foreign” nature. Evangelion’s release on both dubbed and subtitled VHS, beginning only months after the end of the Japanese broadcast and without content edits, refused this binary, and its popularity proselytized anime to a new generation of fans. (This dub, beloved by English-speaking fans but out of circulation since a new version was recorded in 2019, is the option presented on the Criterion Channel, alongside the original Japanese, restoring official access to an important piece of anime history).

title: Google Tells Sites to Fact-Check AI Content Before Publishing
description: Google's guidance on AI-generated content now says to fact-check it by hand before publishing, and the review extends to titles, alt text, and other metadata.
fullText:
Google has updated its guidance for sites that use generative AI, adding a warning that AI output may contain errors and advice to fact-check it by hand before publishing.

Google revised the guidance page on Oct. 1. Its documentation updates page says the change brings the guide in line with the company’s talks at developer events.

The page now extends the manual review to metadata, so teams using AI to write titles or image alt text are covered too.

Google’s new wording goes in the guidance page’s “Focus on accuracy, quality, and relevance” section, right after the section’s opening line. Compared with the Dec. 10, 2025, version, three sentences were added:

“Keep in mind that generative models don’t retrieve facts, but predict a likely sequence of words based on their training data. Because of this, generative AI outputs may contain inaccuracies (also known as hallucinations). It is critical to manually factcheck and review all AI-generated content for accuracy and trustworthiness before publishing.”

In the metadata line that followed, “This includes metadata” became “This review also applies to metadata.” It still lists <title> elements, meta description elements, structured data, and alternate texts for images, “which can appear in Search results.”

Google’s Oct. 1 changelog entry says the generative AI content guide was updated “with information from the Search Quality Raters guidelines.” It’s the only page listed for Oct. 1.

Googlers have recommended fact-checking AI output in public before. I covered an April 2024 Search Off the Record episode in which Gary Illyes said generative AI output always has to be fact-checked. In an August 2025 interview, Illyes said AI content “should be human curated,” with someone checking that it’s accurate, as Roger Montti reported.

The rest of Google’s AI content guidance page matches the Dec. 10, 2025, version. It still opens by saying generative AI can help with research and with adding structure to original content. The same paragraph warns that using AI tools to make many pages without adding value for users may violate the company’s spam policy on scaled content abuse.

The page also still points to sections 4.6.5 and 4.6.6 of the Search Quality Raters guidelines, which cover scaled content abuse and content made with little effort, originality, or added value. It says raters use those guidelines to evaluate Google’s ranking systems and that their ratings “don’t directly influence ranking.”

The Dec. 10, 2025, version of Google’s guidance asked for accuracy but had no manual fact-check instruction for AI output. The Oct. 1 update adds that step and gives Google’s reason for it.

The fact-check step reaches metadata as well as article text. AI-generated metadata, such as title tags, falls under the same manual review as drafts, so a process built only for article copy misses part of what the guidance now covers.

Teams that use AI in content production can now cite Google’s own wording when they set a review policy covering drafts and metadata. The company logs major changes to its Search docs on the documentation updates page, which is the place to watch for further edits.

fullText:
A Russian drone struck a major bridge in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv on Sunday as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in the city to the sound of air raid sirens, explosions and air defense systems being activated.

Merz is in Kyiv to display support for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky amid Russia’s escalation of strikes on the city.

“Ukraine needs all our support in the coming weeks,” Merz said.

Highlighting attacks on Ukraine’s towns, residential buildings and energy, he said: “If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later its war machine will turn ⁠against us.”

Video footage from Sunday morning’s strike showed the moment the city’s Northern Bridge was attacked, sparking a huge plume of fire and black smoke while cars were still traveling across. Two people were injured, the city’s mayor, Vitaliy Klitschko said.

It is the second time the Northern Bridge has been hit in as many days. On Thursday and Friday, Kyiv’s Southern Bridge, which serves ground transportation and the city’s subway system, was hit five times in less than 24 hours.

Ukrainian officials have said that Russian strikes on the capital’s infrastructure are attempting to cut the capital into two, as Kyiv is split along the Dnipro River, with businesses offices and government institutions on the right back, and the left bank mostly residential.

Kyiv plans to start building several alternative crossings over the Dnipro in case the attacks on the bridges continue, the minister of infrastructure said Sunday.

Russia’s defense ministry said it struck the Northern Bridge on Sunday, saying that it was targeting a route used for transporting troops and military equipment. It added that two cargo vessels carrying military equipment to the port of Odesa were struck. On Saturday the Russian Ministry of Defense said that it also targeted a logistics center in the Kyiv region.

Merz visited Kyiv alongside his Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy, Katarina Reiche, despite warnings from Russia on Saturday that foreign visitors and dignitaries to the Ukrainian capital are not safe amid an onslaught of Russian attacks.

Zelensky and Merz are tying up a significant defense and industrial partnership, which will see the two countries finalize a deal for the production of drones and missiles.

Berlin is also expected to release €1 billion ($1.13 billion) in military aid and €350 million ($390 million) for repairs to Ukraine’s damaged energy infrastructure, German government officials said.

Zelensky has warned that Ukraine’s defensive need is expanding amid Russia’s accelerated air campaign, which has seen Moscow fire high-speed, jet-powered Shahed-type drones that can bypass some of Ukraine’s air defense systems and exploit its lack of interceptors.

Earlier on Sunday, Merz said that Ukraine “is facing decisive weeks ahead.” Writing on X, he said: “I have traveled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us.”

Meanwhile, there appears to be no immediate respite for Kyiv’s three million residents, with Moscow on Sunday saying that it will only intensify its strikes targeting the capital and other cities.

“Strikes by the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation against military and military-industrial facilities, as well as associated infrastructure in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine, will be intensified,” the ministry said.

Russia’s renewed threat follows an interview Zelensky gave to Reuters news on Saturday, where he outlined that he plans to double down on attacks on oil refineries.

“We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners, etc. – what gives money to them for this war,” Zelensky said.

His comments come despite the urging of US President Donald Trump, who recently asked Ukraine to stay away from attacks on Russia’s oil infrastructure, claiming it was sending global oil prices surging.

CNN’s Kara Fox and Farida Elsebai contributed reporting.

title: Trump names Jay Clayton as AI czar: Where he stands on AI safety
description:
President Trump on Sunday named Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as his new "AI czar," adding a different category of intelligence, the "artificial" kind, to the U.S. spy chief's portfolio.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump said Clayton will lead a newly formed "Super Intelligence Force" alongside Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor. The group will report directly to Trump and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.
fullText:
President Trump on Sunday named Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as his new "AI czar," adding a different category of intelligence, the "artificial" kind, to the U.S. spy chief's portfolio.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said Clayton will lead a newly formed "Super Intelligence Force" alongside Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor. The group will report directly to Trump and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.

Its goal, Trump wrote, is "to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans."

Clayton will keep his job as DNI, which oversees the nation's 18 intelligence agencies.

Trump's announcement follows meeting last Tuesday at the White House where top AI executives signed what he called a "morally binding" agreement to police themselves in order to prevent their increasingly powerful models from going rogue and harming humanity.

"There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation," the president said at the meeting. "This is going to be all for the good, and we're going to have it be nice and safe."

Despite new polls showing that 86% of Americans want AI companies to meet independent safety standards even if doing so slows development — with 74% largely mistrusting the leaders of those companies — Trump insisted in recent days that federal regulations are unnecessary and that those who say otherwise are "Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers."

"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" he wrote on social media. Elsewhere, Trump has said that regulation would handicap the U.S. in its race to "win" AI.

"Whoever wins AI ... that's the group that wins," Trump told the United Nations General Assembly last month. "We're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way."

According to the Guardian, Trump's previous AI and crypto czar, billionaire tech investor David Sacks, consistently "counseled the president to give a soft touch to AI regulation, helping push executive orders and other measures aimed at loosening restrictions on the technology." Sacks also "maintains direct financial stakes in multiple AI companies," the paper reported, though he took steps to divest some of his holdings last year while serving in the administration. He stepped down in March.

Will Clayton follow Sacks's lead? Or will he chart a new course? Here's what we know so far.

Clayton, 60, is a registered independent with degrees from the University of Pennsylvania (engineering, law) and the University of Cambridge (economics). As a lawyer in private practice, he focused mostly on Wall Street: mergers and acquisitions, market offerings and regulatory proceedings. During Trump's first term, from 2017 to 2020, Clayton chaired the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. From March 2021 to April 2025, Clayton served as chair and "lead independent director" of the board of Apollo Global Management. (Apollo has owned a 90% majority stake in Yahoo since September 2021.)

In late 2024, Trump nominated Clayton to serve as U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, his first prosecutorial job; Trump later appointed Clayton to serve in an acting capacity after New York Sen. Chuck Schumer blocked his appointment. Reports suggest Clayton was also considered for roles as secretary of the treasury, attorney general and director of the Central Intelligence Agency. In November 2025, Trump ordered the Department of Justice to investigate Democrats associated with Jeffrey Epstein, and U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi assigned Clayton to lead the probe.

After former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard resigned in May 2026, Trump tapped Clayton to replace her. "He's very qualified," Democratic Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia said at the time. But Clayton sidestepped questions over who won the 2020 election during his July confirmation hearings, and he was confirmed without Democratic support.

"I'm not an election denier," Clayton told the Senate. "He went through our processes, and Joe Biden became the president of the United States."

During his DNI confirmation hearings, Clayton described AI as "a game changer," warning that it represents "not only an opportunity but a threat."

"We should just all recognize that," he continued. "When something is both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it."

On Tuesday, Clayton attended Trump's White House meeting with top AI executives. Speaking afterward to CNBC, he used the president's new preferred term for AI — i.e., "superintelligence" — while pushing back against lawmakers who have called for regulating or pausing U.S. AI development.

"Super intelligence is a national security issue, and that was something that was recognized yesterday by not just the industry leaders but everybody in the room," Clayton said. "But to, in some way, not try to drive forward inside the United States, with companies that are regulated in the United States ... to somehow say we should back away from this and let the rest of the world develop these models and implement these models? I don't think anybody in that room, and I don't think any American, should think that that's a good strategy."

Asked to respond to criticism from Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts that Trump's current policy of letting AI companies police themselves will prove to be "a recipe for disaster," Clayton suggested that the U.S. government's existing regulatory framework could also help keep AI in check.

"My response to the American people on that front is we have a Federal Trade Commission, we have a Department of Justice," Clayton said. "I know the leaders of both those organizations, and they're committed to protecting the American people in this regard."

According to Trump's post, the Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the federal government's dealings with AI companies, infrastructure providers, consumers, public interest groups and religious organizations, CNN reported.

Last month, Trump wrote on social media that he would "be announcing, in the near future, the AI 'Czar.'

"Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" he added.

In the same post, the president again dismissed concerns about AI safety as a "hoax" perpetrated by "Radical Left Democrats." He also wrote that going forward, his administration would not "in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," which he described as "the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet" — only "even larger and more impactful."

"Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!" Trump explained. As for reining in "bad" actors, he wrote, "we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System."

Clayton, it seems, will now be in charge of cherishing, helping and watching over the AI industry as it grows. He's "a good man," Trump told Axios when the outlet asked last week if Clayton was being considered for the job. "He's right here. That's a good idea."

It's unclear what happened to a separate idea Trump floated last month, which he called "the AI Force."

"I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term," Trump wrote in his September social media post about naming an AI czar.

According to Axios, Trump's AI Force idea "caught advisers by surprise," setting off "a mad dash" within the administration "to imagine what AI Force would look like."

When Sacks served as AI czar, he repeatedly persuaded the president and his administration to resist new AI restrictions, including state laws to limit AI. Since leaving the White House, Sacks has "maintained close ties with the president," according to the Guardian, and "in May, he successfully urged Trump to scrap an executive order that would've subjected AI models to government review."

The Wall Street Journal recently reported the Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles were "caught off guard and unhappy" with Trump's decision after they "spent months negotiating to increase oversight of AI and had consulted a range of industry executives on the order." According to the Journal's sources, Wiles "told others that Sacks had persuaded Trump" to back down "in a last-minute call," leaving Bessent "worried that AI-led cyberattacks could wreak havoc on the nation's banking system."

title: Poll shows Latino voters swinging away from Trump and Republicans
description:
NBC News
Latino voters helped propel Donald Trump back to the White House. Now, they are turning on him, according to a new NBC News/Telemundo poll — a shift that gives Democrats a major opportunity to capitalize in a 2026 election that could hinge on states and districts with sizable Latino populations.
Like the broader electorate, Latino voters are racked by major concerns about high prices and Trump’s approach to immigration enforcement. The president’s approval rating sits at 27% among Latino voters. Two-thirds say his administration’s deportation policies have gone too far and three-quarters disapprove of how he has handled the economy and the cost of living.
fullText:
Latino voters helped propel Donald Trump back to the White House. Now, they are turning on him, according to a new NBC News/Telemundo poll — a shift that gives Democrats a major opportunity to capitalize in a 2026 election that could hinge on states and districts with sizable Latino populations.

Like the broader electorate, Latino voters are racked by major concerns about high prices and Trump’s approach to immigration enforcement. The president’s approval rating sits at 27% among Latino voters. Two-thirds say his administration’s deportation policies have gone too far and three-quarters disapprove of how he has handled the economy and the cost of living.

There are clear signs his party is paying the price.

A greater share of Latino voters hold negative views of the Republican Party than at any time since 2016, and Democrats have leads on issues like dealing with the economy, immigration, the cost of living, corruption and healthcare. Two years ago, Latino voters gave Trump a 4-point edge over then-Vice President Kamala Harris on handling the economy. Today, they give Democrats a 21-point advantage on the same question.

Against that backdrop, Democrats have a 24-point lead on whom Latino voters want to see in control of Congress, 59%-35%.

That’s double the lead they had among Latino voters at this point in 2024, though not quite at the heights the party enjoyed at this time in 2018, according to NBC News polling from just before that election.

Nearly a fifth of Latino voters who backed Trump in 2024 say they do not prefer a Republican-controlled Congress, with 14% saying they support Democrats and 8% unsure in their preference.

The shifts come after the Republican Party made Trump’s 2024 gains among Latino voters central to its plans to keep the House majority. In Florida and Texas, the party drew new, heavily Latino districts that looked deep red by the 2024 results — but many are shaping up to be competitive in the midterms as Latino voters’ preferences have changed. Statewide races in Texas, Nevada and more will also be shaped by the evolving Latino vote, though it will not move as one bloc everywhere in the country.

The poll results, collected Sept. 21-28, “indicate a striking reversal of Republican gains with Latino voters and point to trouble ahead for Republican candidates in the midterms,” said Democratic pollster Aileen Cardona-Arroyo of Hart Research Associates, who conducted the poll with Republican pollster Micah Roberts and his firm, Public Opinion Strategies. Latino voters comprised around a tenth of the total vote in recent midterm elections.

Roberts referred to Latino voters as “the swingiest of swing groups,” calling the reversal since 2024 “stunning.”

“What we can really say from this data is that 2024 was the outlier,” he said, adding: “Trump is a central figure. He’s had real consequences on our politics, and without his presence, I think none of these changes would be evident in the data among Latinos.”

But the results among Latino voters are not all good news for Democrats, who have not seen their party’s image improve in two years. And while Democrats have a midterm lead, Republicans are pulling more Latino support than in any NBC News poll before the 2024 election cycle, too, dating back to 2012.

“Despite a more favorable environment for Democrats, any Democratic gains this November will be driven largely more by opposition to Trump and the economic environment than by support for Democrats,” Arroyo-Cardona said.

Latino voters overwhelmingly disapprove of the president’s handling of the cost of living (78%), the economy (74%), foreign policy (68%) and immigration (69%). Trump’s best issue of the five tested is border security — where 39% approve and 58% disapprove of his handling.

His marks on foreign policy, the economy and cost of living are significantly lower than where then-President Joe Biden sat with Latino voters in September 2022, when Democrats had a better-than-expected midterm result despite losing control of the House. Then, 60% disapproved of Biden’s handling of the cost of living and 54% disapproved of his handling of the economy.

Nearly two-thirds (65%) of Latino voters say the president’s policies have hurt economic conditions, compared with 23% who say his policies have helped and 11% who say they haven’t made much of a difference.

Among Latino independents, just 10% believe his policies have helped the economy, while 72% believe his policies have hurt it.

Meanwhile, inflation and the cost of living ranked as the most important issue to 33% of Latino voters. That made it the top issue in the survey — and a majority (52%) ranked it as the most or second-most important issue.

Latino voters who say the cost of living is the most important issue also prefer a Democratic Congress by 22 points. That’s a shift from the 2024 poll, when Republicans had a 4-point edge among these voters.

A sizable majority of Latinos (63%) say their family’s income is falling behind the cost of living, while 25% say it is staying even and 11% say it is going up faster than the cost of living, similar to findings in 2024.

Luisa Santiago, a 59-year-old Florida retiree who participated in the survey, told NBC News in a subsequent interview that she voted for Trump in 2024 after a lifetime of voting for Democrats and convinced many of her friends to do the same. She was frustrated with the Democrats on the economy and on transgender issues.

“It was a big deal when we voted for Republicans, and then we feel like it was a complete mistake,” she said, calling Trump a “disappointment.”

“I’m more embarrassed than my friends because I was the one who convinced them to vote for him,” she added.

Santiago lambasted the president’s deportation policies as “brutal” and “cold,” while also saying the difficult economic climate is weighing heavily on her and her family.

While immigration didn’t rank as highly on the priority list, Latino voters expressed similar frustration with Trump’s hard-edged deportation policies.

Two-thirds say Trump’s immigration enforcement measures have gone too far, 22% say he’s struck the right approach, and 9% say he hasn’t gone far enough.

While 83% support deporting all undocumented immigrants who have committed serious crimes, just 37% support deporting every undocumented immigrant in the U.S.

Roberts, the Republican pollster, pointed to the difference between support for deporting serious criminals and deporting everyone in America illegally as he imagined “what might have been” for Republicans.

“There is support for a certain level of immigration enforcement, but the Latino electorate believes it’s gone way too far,” he added.

In the poll, 31% of Latino voters say they or someone close to them started carrying identification over concerns about ICE enforcement, while 27% say they know someone who has been deported or detained by ICE in the last two years.

Eighteen percent say they or someone close to them has considered leaving the U.S. over the last two years over concerns about ICE enforcement, and 17% say they or someone close to them has considered not voting in person this year because of concerns about ICE.

Maria, a Florida voter in her 20s who responded to the poll, told NBC News in a follow-up interview that Trump has “fallen short” in the two years since she voted for him. She declined to share her last name while discussing politics.

She highlighted frustration on the economy and on deportations, arguing that while Trump promised to deport the worst of the worst, “I’ve had many friends, family members deported.”

“They were supposed to be here. They had paperwork, and it didn’t matter. And now they can never come back. One of my friend’s grandpas didn’t even get deported to his home country. He got deported to Mexico instead of Cuba,” she later added.

The numbers for Trump and Republicans could spell trouble in November in states and districts with sizable Latino populations.

“In a lot of the heavily Hispanic and Latino districts across the country that Trump and Republicans did well, and better than ever in, in 2024, you’re going to see that reversal,” said Roberts, the Republican pollster, noting Trump’s tough numbers on immigration and the cost of living.

“This entire poll is full of very clear directional signals that Latinos have turned from 2024 and are ready to make a different choice with regard to who’s in control of Congress,” Roberts said.

Democrats’ 24-point lead on the generic congressional ballot is twice as large as their margin in the 2024 version of the poll. But it’s not nearly as wide as the 43-point lead the party enjoyed at this point in the 2018 midterms.

Latino voters also now say Democrats would better handle the cost of living and the economy by significant margins, erasing the advantages Trump and Republicans have enjoyed in past elections.

Latino voters favor Democrats to handle other issues, and they break even on which party would better handle border security. More voters also say Democrats are more likely than Republicans to share their values and address the concerns of the Hispanic community.

Amid the economic frustrations, voters are also more motivated to head to the polls in November. A sizable majority (72%) rank themselves a 10 out of 10 in terms of interest in November’s elections, compared with 54% at this time in 2024. Meanwhile, 62% say they are more motivated to vote this year than in midterms past.

And a majority (54%) say their midterm vote is meant to send a signal of opposition to Trump, while 21% say they want to signal their support for Trump and 23% say their vote is not about sending a signal to the president either way.

While the poll results offer plenty of short-term upside for Democrats, they also outline longer-term changes trending against the party.

While Latino voters’ negative views of the GOP have jumped since 2024, views of the Democratic Party have not improved. Now, 62% of Latino voters have negative views of the Republican Party, a 16-point increase from two years ago, while 42% have a negative view of the Democratic Party, a 4-point increase from 2024.

“I’m still wary about the Democratic Party because I don’t really know that much other than what I was fed,” said Maria, the Florida voter in her 20s, before adding that she’s still leaning toward voting for Democrats: “I feel like I have to put my faith in them now to fix things.”

She said she voted for Trump in 2024 in large part because her family instilled a fear of socialism and Democrats in her.

The poll found that socialism remains underwater with Latino voters — 13% feel positively about it and 41% view socialism negatively, with 38 feeling neutral about socialism.

Cardona-Arroyo, the Democratic pollster, noted that the party has work to do after the midterms to develop a broader message.

“What do Democrats do to move beyond this place where they’re running on opposition to the Republican Party, which I think will work in ’26,” Cardona-Arroyo said. “It’s sort of an open question of whether that will work in ’28.”

The NBC News/Telemundo poll surveyed 800 registered Latino voters Sept. 21-28 via a mix of telephone interviews and an online survey sent via text messages. Overall, 20% of the interviews were conducted in Spanish. The poll has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points.

7 men were accused of sexual assault at Cornell. Here's how the school responded.
description:
Two of the seven men accused of sexually assaulting a Cornell University student at a fraternity house in 2024 were expelled, while others were ordered to take sexual harassment training and write "reflection papers," according to university disciplinary records obtained by the New York Times.
The records offer the most detailed look yet at how Cornell handled the case, which has drawn national outrage and is now under criminal investigation by New York Attorney General Letitia James.
On Friday, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said that a woman who alleges she was drugged and raped by multiple members of a Cornell University fraternity in 2024 was "failed" by those obligated to protect her.
Hochul's comments came a day after announcing she had lost faith in the district attorney overseeing the Cornell University rape case and signed an executive order appointing James as a special prosecutor to lead the investigation.
fullText:
Two of the seven men accused of sexually assaulting a Cornell University student at a fraternity house in 2024 were expelled, while others were ordered to take sexual harassment training and write "reflection papers," according to university disciplinary records obtained by the New York Times.

The records offer the most detailed look yet at how Cornell handled the case, which has drawn national outrage and is now under criminal investigation by New York Attorney General Letitia James.

On Friday, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said that a woman who alleges she was drugged and raped by multiple members of a Cornell University fraternity in 2024 was "failed" by those obligated to protect her.

Hochul's comments came a day after announcing she had lost faith in the district attorney overseeing the Cornell University rape case and signed an executive order appointing James as a special prosecutor to lead the investigation.

"In what world would the police learn from a victim that she'd been literally gang raped while intoxicated by five men in a fraternity house and not elevate those allegations to the district attorney?" Hochul said at a press conference with James in New York. "In what world does the district attorney not even interview her or anyone else involved or even request the full transcript?

"At every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her," Hochul said.

James said that the case is "now an active criminal investigation."

"We will review the facts, gather evidence, interview witnesses and, if warranted, pursue prosecutions," James said, adding: "I know that you want answers. I do too."

The local district attorney and Cornell both said they support James taking over the case.

Read more from Yahoo: A timeline of the Cornell rape case, from the alleged 2024 incident to the appointment of a special prosecutor to oversee the criminal investigation

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has come under intense scrutiny in recent days over his decision not to prosecute anyone when the initial allegations were made in 2024.

In a civil lawsuit filed last month against the school and seven current and former fraternity members, a former student identified as "Jane Doe" alleged that she was the victim of a "gang rape" at the Chi Phi fraternity on Cornell's Ithaca, N.Y., campus on Oct. 19, 2024. She said she was already intoxicated when she arrived and was given ketamine before and during the alleged assault. She reported the incident to campus police three weeks later.

Van Houten said last week that Jane Doe's sworn statement to police didn't include allegations that she was "drugged against her will or gang raped."

"On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual," Van Houten said. "My office obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later."

On Tuesday, CBS New York published excerpts from Jane Doe's Nov. 14, 2024, interview with Cornell police, in which she asserted, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."

"Shockingly, those words never made it into the account that the Cornell police sent to prosecutors," Hochul said Friday.

Van Houten said he was not provided with a transcript of her interview before his office decided not to pursue charges.

"I'm going to follow up on this because this is news to me," Van Houten told CBS. "If she had said those words, we certainly would want to have explored that more. Like I said, that wasn't provided to me."

Records obtained by the New York Times show the district attorney's office declined to look at additional evidence gathered by Cornell police beyond Jane Doe's six-page statement. A Cornell police investigator wrote in a note that prosecutors had already decided, based on that statement, that "criminal charges would not be pursued in this case."

Van Houten told the Times in an email that the other records were "not pertinent to our analysis because we had Jane Doe's comprehensive account of the events."

Cornell initially said its police "shared all investigatory information" with the district attorney's office. The university later revised its statement to say police shared "the victim's sworn statement and the Snapchat screenshot," CNN reported.

According to ABC News, Jane Doe told the school's investigators that she "felt like bait" on the night of the alleged assault.

"I felt like lions around me," she said during a 2025 hearing. "It just was a totally debilitating place to be in."

The comments were included in a 99-page report prepared by the university as part of its Title IX investigation, per ABC.

The report also included comments from a fraternity member who Cornell's investigation concluded did not engage in the assault but was found responsible for "attempted sexual exploitation."

"I was sorry that maybe if it wasn't consensual and she was victimized, I was sorry for not stopping it," the fraternity member said, according to ABC.

That student, who was allowed to stay at Cornell, has asked a New York court to throw out the disciplinary finding against him, the Associated Press reported. His punishment included a no-contact order, a class on sexual harassment and bystander intervention, and a reflection paper.

Two of the men have released statements through their lawyers denying they participated in a sexual assault, according to the Associated Press.

Cornell University issued a statement pushing back against claims that the school did not thoroughly punish those involved in the alleged assault.

"Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false," the university said. "A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault."

Hochul announced on Wednesday that Cornell had agreed to initiate an independent review of its initial response to the allegations.

The governor also said she would work to close a loophole in New York law, which states that someone who was voluntarily intoxicated cannot claim they were mentally incapacitated during an assault, unless they can show they were "physically helpless" and unable to communicate consent.

"If someone is too intoxicated to consent, it should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol," Hochul said. "Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape. Period."

On Sept. 14, Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against Cornell University and seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity, alleging that she was the victim of a "gang rape" at the fraternity house when she was incapable of consent — and that the school failed to protect her from "sexual predators" on its campus.

The defendants named in the lawsuit include Cornell, the seven fraternity members, the Chi Phi fraternity, the woman's own sorority, Delta Delta Delta, and an off-campus bar that allegedly served her alcohol.

She is seeking unspecified compensatory and punitive damages resulting from "sustained psychological injuries, severe emotional distress, along with pain and suffering and loss of enjoyment of life."

According to her lawsuit, Jane Doe was a 20-year-old student at the school in October 2024 when she went to visit a friend at the fraternity house on Cornell's Ithaca, N.Y., campus while intoxicated. Shortly after arriving, Jane Doe alleged that she was pressured by two fraternity brothers into snorting what they said was ketamine before sexually assaulting her. One of the men then allegedly sent a message to the fraternity's Snapchat group suggesting that she was available for sex. A screengrab of part of the chat was included in the lawsuit.

According to the complaint, multiple other members of the fraternity showed up, and she was raped for hours.

"The Snapchat was disgusting and vulgar and immoral," Van Houten told ABC News. "But the question that we analyzed was, did Jane Doe consent to what happened? And the law in New York state is clear: That if you are voluntarily intoxicated, or under the influence of drugs such that your judgment is impaired, that does not legally under the penal law constitute your inability to consent."

During the alleged assault, the fraternity members "began pouring lines of Ketamine all over her body and snorting them," according to the complaint.

"At around 5:45 AM, this assault concluded and Plaintiff lost consciousness," the lawsuit stated.

About three weeks later, on Nov. 8, 2024, Jane Doe reported the incident to the university's police department.

According to ABC News, Jane Doe told police in a sworn statement on Nov. 15, 2024, that the incident "felt like coercion," and that at one point she said "no to the foursome" one of the fraternity brothers had proposed. She also stated: "I felt like I was unable to make any decision because of how intoxicated I was."

According to the New York Times, she told Cornell's Title IX investigators that she did not consider herself a victim until she saw the incident being discussed in an online forum.

"Are Chi Phi brothers Crips or Bloods because I hear they have been doing hell Gang Banging?" one user wrote.

"They do drugs and gang r*ped a sophomore," wrote another.

"That's the first time I had ever heard the narrative change that I wasn't a whore and that I was assaulted," Jane Doe told investigators, per the Times.

Cornell's months-long Title IX investigation included at least 12 hearings, according to the lawsuit, which said that the accused fraternity members were "afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell."

The panel's sanctions varied widely, according to the records obtained by the Times:

Two men were expelled. The panel found one responsible for sexual assault, concluding he had manipulated and endangered Jane Doe. The other had been accused of assault and of sending the Snapchat message that drew other fraternity members to the room.

Two were suspended, one for two years and one for three semesters, followed by probation. Both were barred from contacting Jane Doe and ordered to complete sexual harassment training and write reflection papers.

One, who had already graduated, was barred from campus for three years. Jane Doe had accused him of forcibly kissing her.

Two received lighter sanctions: no-contact orders, training on sexual harassment, social media use and bystander intervention, and reflection papers.

Cornell has denied that essays were the only punishment for any of the men. All seven deny wrongdoing, and none has been criminally charged. Jane Doe dropped out of school.

In a video message Saturday, Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff said the university's board would name an outside law firm this week to review how the school handled the case. He also promised "a serious look" at fraternities and sororities, the Cornell Daily Sun reported.

On Sept. 21, Cornell issued a statement saying that it had concluded its Title IX investigation but would not disclose individual sanctions, citing federal privacy laws.

"The Cornell Office of Civil Rights and the Office of Student Conduct and Community Standards investigated and adjudicated the allegations consistent with university policies. The Xi chapter of Chi Phi fraternity remains barred from our campus," the statement said: "Federal privacy law prohibits Cornell from disclosing specific information regarding individual students and we therefore are unable to make a public statement on any other disciplinary response. Violations of university policies could lead to sanctions up to and including suspension or expulsion. We will respond in detail through the legal process."

The university also pointed out that it launched a task force on campus sexual assault in the wake of the incident and issued a report in March with recommendations for "an environment that fosters sexual health and safety."

"Several of the recommendations have already been implemented, while others are in development with oversight by a university implementation committee," Cornell said.

According to USA Today, more than 1,200 incidents of sexual assault, domestic and dating violence and stalking were reported to Cornell University's Title IX from 2018 through 2024. Of those, 14 cases resulted in suspensions, while seven ended in expulsion or dismissal, per the paper.

"Cornell takes each report seriously and, to the greatest extent possible, honors a complainant's decision not to pursue resolution," Rebecca Valli, a Cornell spokesperson, said in a statement to USA Today. "The university provides support and resources regardless of whether the respondent is subject to our conduct processes, and regardless of whether a complainant consents to an investigation."

The harrowing allegations revealed in Jane Doe's lawsuit prompted reactions from several celebrities, including Florence Pugh, who posted a lengthy response on Instagram calling for men to speak out against sexual violence.

"This is really the moment where we need our men to be as horrified and as sickened as us," Pugh wrote. "You need to be leading conversations about how we change the allowance and complicity of this behaviour as much as we are. How can you expect us to trust that it's 'not all men' when in moments like this, many of you stay quiet?"

In an expletive-laden Instagram post, actor Josh Gad tore into Cornell, seizing on allegations in the civil lawsuit that the fraternity members were required to write essays as part of the adjudication process.

"When we start setting a precedent that our girls and women can be brutally raped, and the resulting disciplinary action is to hand out (checks notes) ESSAYS (like it's Bart Simpson being a lil' rascal), about why it was wrong to brutally violate an innocent girl, we have lost our f***ing minds," Gad wrote.

Toby Morton, a former South Park writer, launched a website, TheCornell7.org, dedicated to holding the school and the accused fraternity members accountable.

"Accountability is coming," Morton wrote on Instagram.

Mariska Hargitay posted a joint statement on Instagram with the Joyful Heart Foundation, which supports survivors of sexual assault, domestic violence, and child abuse, with a quote from a scathing editorial by the Cornell Daily Sun.

"Arrest them," Heated Rivalry star Hudson Williams wrote in an Instagram story while sharing a photo of the seven accused men, according to Variety.

"F*** them and f*** Cornell, too!" he added.

At a town hall in Ithaca, N.Y., last week, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a New York Democrat, said that "the culture of rape, sexual assault and pedophilia is protected in elite institutions across the United States, including Cornell."

Ocasio-Cortez recalled her own experience as a freshman at Boston University.

"Within maybe 10 seconds of me walking into a party — at a gym, at a school facility — someone had touched me inappropriately," Ocasio-Cortez said.

"Jane Doe, that survivor, lost her education because you can't stay in school when something like that happens to you," Ocasio-Cortez told the crowd. "She had to lose her education, and those men were protected by an institution and granted an Ivy League degree as a reward. Never again."

The congresswoman said she had a message to Jane Doe and other survivors of sexual assault.

"I want you to know that you are not defined by the things that have happened to you," Ocasio-Cortez said. "You are bigger than that. You are stronger than them. And they will never define you for your entire life. And that you can achieve anything that you want to achieve, from one survivor to another."

title: 2 dead and 35 injured in mass shooting at Georgia homecoming celebration
description:
Multiple law enforcement agencies responded to a mass shooting from early Sunday morning, leading to two deaths and dozens injured.

fullText:
Multiple law enforcement agencies responded to a mass shooting from early Sunday morning, leading to two deaths and dozens injured.

Dooly County Coroner Brett Walls told WALB and WMAZ that two people were dead, a 20-year-old man and a 23-year-old man in Vienna, two hours south of Atlanta.

Sheriff Craig Peavy told WALB and WMAZ that the Vienna shooting happened during a homecoming celebration from Saturday night and into early Sunday.

The sheriff told WMAZ that as many as 25 people were taken to the hospital for treatment of their injuries.

It is still unclear if any suspects are being sought or in custody, nor is a possible motive for the shooting known.

Tries: Jibulu, O'Flaherty, Bamber Cons: Ford 2, Lozowski

Sale overcame Jacques Vermeulen's red card to defeat Saracens and pick up their first win of The Prem campaign.

Sarries struggled to break down a stubborn Sharks defence despite having numerical superiority for 27 minutes of the first half after Alex Lozowski's yellow and Vermeulen's 20-minute red card.

Incredibly, Sale took a 7-5 lead into half-time thanks to Nathan Jibulu's early converted try, despite Eroni Mawi's reply, and then went further ahead soon after the break as Tom O'Flaherty raced in.

Ben Bamber stretched Sale's lead to 11 points after Sione Va'enuku had cut the gap, and though Charlie Bracken's late score again put the game in the balance, the hosts held on.

After shipping 150 points to Saracens in two Prem hammerings last season, Sale's victory at the Stone X was built on a huge defensive effort.

Their forwards laid down an impressive early marker when a driving maul carved through Sarries with relative ease to sweep Jibulu over the line.

But the visitors were soon down to 13 as former Sarrie Alex Lozowski was yellow-carded for a high shot on Barbeary on his first Sale start before Vermeulen was red-carded for putting a shoulder into Tomos Williams' head.

And only a TMO intervention prevented the visitors going down to 12 when Hamish Smales overturned Courtney Lawes' yellow card for a deliberate knock on.

Smales was involved again to overturn Nick Tompkins' smart close-range finish for a Nick Isiekwe's obstruction in the build-up, but Mawi finally turned Sarries' red-zone pressure into points when he powered over.

Yet Sale were heartened to head into half-time with a two-point lead and back up to full strength as Elia Canakaivata replaced Vermeulen.

Saracens responded with three changes at half-time, including a debut for England lock George Martin, but Sale soon went nine points clear when O'Flaherty collected George Ford's up and under on halfway and raced away to score.

The hosts finally found their cutting edge when a quick switch of play while camped on the Sale line created an overlap and gave Va'Enuku a walk-in on debut.

Sale's defence continued to impress before a quick change of pace in attack sent them 21-10 up as Ford teed up Bamber to run a hard line through a gap and race in.

Once again the Sarries response was swift as Jack Bracken cut in off the right wing to give brother Charlie a clear run to the line to set up a tense finale.

Despite opening the season with an eventful and impressive 40-38 win over Leicester, Brendan Venter made most of the headlines in its aftermath.

The former South Africa international was reported to have changed his job title to head of rugby culture and wine consultant after failing to follow media commitments at the league's season launch and opening match.

Sarries new chief executive Ed Coetzee on Friday ended the confusion on Friday by confirming Venter as head of culture and technical director, a role which will include "significant media duties".

Venter duly spoke to TNT Sports before the clash with Sale and said he refused the director's title because he had "absolutely nothing" to do with other sections of the club such as the academy and women's section.

The 56-year-old also insisted the wine consultant reference was not a joke aimed at the media.

"Our whole theme this year was all about wine," Venter told TNT Sports. "Everything in our theme was about a blend and getting the blend right.

"There's nobody in life that is successful by doing one thing the whole time, it doesn't work like that. As you grow older you have to blend things so that's where it came from, and it's very relevant."

Chris Jones, BBC Rugby Union correspondent

The Prem has been all about free flowing attack so far this season, but this was much more of an old school dogfight.

A stop-start game dominated by the referee's whistle, Sale came up with two big plays in the second half: Tom O'Flaherty with a stunning individual score, while Ben Bamber's try was also a beauty after excellent build-up play.

The big names stepped up for Sale. Courtney Lawes looked his old self in the lineout and on the floor, while Tom Curry was magnificent in the kind of physical scrap he relishes. George Ford managed the game beautifully in the closing stages.

Sarries director of rugby turned wine consultant turned technical director Brendan Venter again handed media duties over to head coach Joe Shaw post-match, but he will talk this week in a bid to avoid further sanctions from Prem Rugby.

"We couldn't really get into our flow, that's the truth of it. Credit to Sale, they came and fronted up.

"They had adversity, which we had last weekend, but they kept coming. We have to take it on the chin and move on."

Sale director of rugby Alex Sanderson:

"Any time you watch Nathan (Jibulu) play he makes an impact.

"He was a wrecking ball and caused havoc around the field. He nailed his line-outs and showed he's of international class.

"You can get away with being fast and skilful in the Prem, but it's another level again in terms of the power that's required at international level and he's got that ability. He's immensely strong.

"This could be the season when he explodes onto the international scene."
