title: Elena Rybakina confirms her withdrawal from her next tournament after shock defeat in Beijing, ‘I’m very sorry’
description: Elena Rybakina will not be playing at the Wuhan Open this year after withdrawing from the upcoming tournament. Rybakina has just suffered a shock defeat...
fullText:
Elena Rybakina will not be playing at the Wuhan Open this year after withdrawing from the upcoming tournament.

Rybakina has just suffered a shock defeat at the China Open to world number 118 Alina Charaeva, and afterwards admitted she was hampered by an ongoing left foot issue.

This defeat saw Rybakina become part of unwanted WTA history, as just the second WTA player in history to lose their first match as world number one.

Following this loss, Rybakina has confirmed that she will not be playing at her next tournament in Wuhan, in a statement released by the tournament.

Rybakina has confirmed that the reason for her withdrawal from the Wuhan Open is related to her ongoing foot issue, as she apologised to her fans after pulling out from the tournament.

"I'm very sorry to the fans who were looking forward to seeing me play," said Rybakina, in a statement on the Wuhan Open's Instagram. "I'll take some time to rest and recover. Thank you for your understanding and continued support. See you next year."

Rybakina reached the quarter-finals at the Wuhan Open last year, and will subsequently drop all 215 points from her ranking that she earned from this run.

The foot issue that Rybakina is currently dealing with also puts her in doubt for the rest of the Asian swing, as she is also entered into the Ningbo Open, Tokyo Open and the year-end WTA Finals. This is a part of the season where Rybakina did very well last year, and therefore it could give Aryna Sabalenka an opportunity to close the gap on the world number one.

However, Sabalenka also suffered an early loss at the China Open and will be hoping to redeem herself as the now confirmed top seed in Wuhan.

title: Report: Liverpool interested in move for Brighton forward
description: Kaoru Mitoma Transfer Latest: Tottenham Reunion Talk Grows as Liverpool Monitor Brighton Contract Stand-offKaoru Mitoma is moving into a delicate phase of his Brighton career, and the sense around the...
fullText:
Kaoru Mitoma is moving into a delicate phase of his Brighton career, and the sense around the market is that his situation could become one of the more attractive opportunities for leading clubs over the coming windows. According to TeamTalk, Tottenham and Liverpool are among those keeping a close eye on developments as the winger approaches the final stretch of his current deal.

Mitoma's contract position is what makes this especially relevant. The Japan international is entering the last season of his agreement at Brighton, and while there had been hope earlier in the year that fresh terms could be agreed, there has been no meaningful breakthrough. For Brighton, that naturally sharpens the decision-making. They can look to protect value in the market, or hold their nerve and risk seeing an important player edge closer to leaving for nothing.

The 29-year-old signed a four-year extension in October 2023 through to 30 June 2027, on around £80,000 a week, placing him among the stronger earners at the club. Yet the picture has changed. Interest from elsewhere appears to be a significant factor, and the longer discussions drift, the more realistic an exit begins to feel.

One strand to watch is Tottenham. The possibility of a reunion with Roberto De Zerbi gives the story a degree of logic, particularly given their previous work together at Brighton. Familiarity matters in recruitment, especially when a coach wants players capable of adapting quickly to specific tactical demands.

Spurs have already committed heavily to reshaping the squad under De Zerbi, and while the broader form has yet to fully reflect that investment, Mitoma could represent a practical addition if the price is favourable. A winter move on reduced terms would appeal if Tottenham believe he can make an immediate impact in the second half of the campaign.

There is also a broader context to Tottenham's attacking planning, with the club linked to further forward options from Asia. That does not diminish the Mitoma angle, but it does suggest they are surveying the market with purpose rather than focusing on a single target.

Liverpool's interest is not new. Their recruitment operation admired Mitoma before his move from Kawasaki Frontale to Brighton, and that long-term appreciation has not disappeared. As his contract winds down, the profile becomes even more appealing, a proven Premier League winger, high-level one-versus-one threat, and a player who may become available below normal market rate.

That said, monitoring a situation and acting on it are very different things. Liverpool will weigh age, wages, fitness and squad need, particularly under Andoni Iraola as he settles into the role. Mitoma's quality is established, but any club considering a move will want reassurance on availability before accelerating.

Brighton's challenge is made more complicated by Mitoma's recovery. A hamstring injury suffered in May ended his 2025-26 season and also ruled him out of the World Cup, leaving him on a cautious rehabilitation programme. Until he is back playing regularly and showing his usual sharpness, the level of January urgency may be reduced.

That opens the door to multiple outcomes. Brighton could still find a buyer prepared to move early, especially if the fee reflects the contract risk. Equally, clubs may decide the smarter play is patience, with several Champions League-level sides already reported to have explored the possibility of waiting for a free transfer in 2027.

Beyond England, Bayern Munich remain a club repeatedly mentioned around Mitoma, and there has also been interest elsewhere in Europe. For now, though, the central point is straightforward. Brighton are running short of time to regain control of the situation, and clubs such as Tottenham and Liverpool are well placed to observe, assess and strike only if the conditions become favourable.

From a Liverpool perspective, this feels like one of those reports that makes sense on paper but still leaves plenty of room for doubt. Mitoma is a very good player, proven in the Premier League and capable of producing moments that shift matches. If the fee dropped low enough, it would be easy to understand why Liverpool would at least discuss it internally.

At the same time, there are clear reservations. He is 29, coming back from a hamstring problem, and Liverpool have to be very careful about where they place resources during a period of transition. Iraola will want intensity, availability and tactical reliability from his wide players, and any recruitment decision has to align with that long term rather than simply reacting to a market opportunity.

An unsure Liverpool fan would probably land somewhere in the middle. There is obvious talent there, and there is reassurance in the fact the club have liked him for years. Yet this cannot be purely about grabbing a bargain because a contract is running down. Liverpool need certainty more than temptation.

If Mitoma returns strongly and Brighton become open to sensible terms, the interest would be understandable. If the cost rises or the fitness picture remains unclear, stepping back may be the wiser move. It is an intriguing one, but perhaps not yet a convincing one.

title: DeChambeau Faces Steep Hurdle In PGA Tour Return
description: Analysis shows Bryson DeChambeau's return to the PGA Tour is unlikely as LIV 2.0 promotion creates friction with board members and strict conditions.
fullText:
Brooks Koepka walked back onto the PGA Tour stage in January, sparking a wave of hope that the rift between tours might finally be healing. It looked like the start of a mass exodus from LIV Golf. But that wave never came. The tour extended the same return invitation to Bryson DeChambeau, Jon Rahm, and Cameron Smith.

None of them took the bait. Koepka's move now stands alone, a one-off exception rather than a new trend. This silence raises a tough question for the game: if these stars want to come back, will they actually be welcome? The answer depends on who they are and what they did.

According to Yahoo Sports, the situation is far more complex for DeChambeau than for others. While Koepka returned, the path for the former U.S. Open champion looks blocked. Eamon Lynch, writing for Golfweek, offered a blunt assessment of the landscape. He noted that not every player would find it easy to rejoin the tour.

According to reports, PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp could internally advocate for players who enhance the product. Examples cited by him include Jon Rahm, Tyrrell Hatton, Cam Smith, and Joaquin Niemann. However, these names represent Lynch's own examples rather than a list officially confirmed by the PGA Tour. This distinction holds significance, particularly regarding DeChambeau's potential position should he ever attempt to return.

The barriers for a return are not just about skill; they are about money and perception. Lynch posits that any player wishing to return must demonstrate sufficient humility to acknowledge their prior choice was erroneous. Such individuals would also need to surrender their equity, or ownership stake in the Tour's business, for a long duration, possibly forever. This is a massive financial ask.

Furthermore, Lynch thinks any returning player might be asked to provide a significant charitable donation. He expects this sum to far surpass Koepka's reported $5 million contribution. These expectations from Lynch outline what a potential return might demand, not conditions officially established by the tour.

Yahoo Sports reports that the promotion of LIV Golf 2.0 has rubbed board members the wrong way. DeChambeau is often at the center of that controversy. The prevailing view is that he constitutes a liability that nobody wants to take on. This phrase comes directly from Lynch's column. It highlights the deep friction between the two organizations.

While Rahm and Smith might be viewed as assets who could draw crowds, DeChambeau's brand is tied to the very division the tour wants to move past. The tour extended the same return opportunity to Bryson DeChambeau, Jon Rahm, and Cameron Smith, but none elected to move. Their silence speaks volumes about the current climate.

The golf world watches these moves closely. The fans want to see the best players compete together. But the business reality is cold. If DeChambeau wants to return, he faces a mountain of obstacles. He must give up his stake in a rival tour and likely pay a heavy price in charity. He must also navigate the optics of his past actions.

Lynch's view suggests that the door is not closed, but it is heavily guarded. The tour is looking for players who fit a specific narrative. DeChambeau does not currently fit that mold. His return is unlikely as long as the current tensions persist. The board members are not eager to take on the baggage he carries.

Until the tour changes its stance or DeChambeau changes his approach, the split remains. The Koepka return was a surprise. A DeChambeau return would be a shock.

title: Jimmie Johnson’s Legacy Goes Beyond NASCAR’s Record Books
description: Seven NASCAR championships and 83 wins made Jimmie Johnson a legend. Twenty years of philanthropy with his wife, Chandra, have given his legacy another dimension.
fullText:
In 2006, Jimmie Johnson was beginning to look like a man who might rewrite the NASCAR record books. He won five races that season, bringing his career total to 23, and captured the first of what would eventually become seven NASCAR Cup Series championships. The sport had a new dominant force, although even Johnson couldn't have known just how far that journey would take him.

That same year, Johnson and his wife, Chandra, started the Jimmie Johnson Foundation, turning their commitment to charitable causes into an organization focused primarily on supporting K-12 public education. Twenty years later, the foundation has invested more than $13.7 million in public schools and nonprofit organizations, helping children, families and communities across the country.

For Johnson, the foundation has also provided lessons that extend well beyond philanthropy. In particular, he's learned what happens when people believe in a cause and see that the person behind it is genuinely committed.

"It's amazing how people show up for you," Johnson said. "Kyle Petty gave me a bunch of advice and helped us with the confidence to formalize the foundation. And my wife and I were both very active in charities and supporting other causes. And he gave us the confidence to start our own charity, our own foundation, and that people would show up, especially if they knew you were passionate about the cause. And people will show up if you're there."

The foundation recently held its annual golf tournament in Charlotte, North Carolina, continuing a tradition that brings supporters together around its mission. And Johnson says the experience of building the organization has influenced how he approaches his role as majority owner of Legacy Motor Club.

"Gosh, it's where I am today as a team owner," he said. "Because I'm really here leading this team, people are showing up. It's wild, these different experiences along the way."

The connection, Johnson believes, comes down to something that applies equally to charitable work, business and competition: people matter. You can have the money, the machinery and the grand plan, but none of it amounts to much without people willing to get behind it.

"If you could distill it down far enough, there's a few attributes that matter in personal life, charitable space, business life, the competitor behind the wheel, and it's people show up if your heart's in it," he said. "And that's really been the story of the foundation and been so impressed with how people have shown up to support us."

Over two decades, Johnson has seen the impact of that support through the schools and individuals the foundation has helped. The results aren't always captured neatly in a balance sheet or a trophy cabinet. Sometimes they're found in a school's arts or music department, an athletics program, or a student whose opportunities have changed because someone provided the resources to make a difference.

"We've always been focused on children and of course, the families associated and the communal elements to it," he said. "Many, many incredible experiences but to impact someone's life and we still stay in contact with so many of the individuals we supported or the schools. The effect that our contributions have made in their arts department and music department, athletics, we've had a few different causes we've supported over time, but to help people and to stay in contact with those individuals, you see that you really, really help someone and help somebody change the direction of their life. That part is everything."

Johnson is scheduled to make his final NASCAR Cup Series start at the 2027 Daytona 500, returning to the No. 48 Chevrolet that became synonymous with his championship years. His 83 victories and seven titles will remain in the record books, where statistics have a habit of becoming increasingly tidy with the passage of time. What happens next, however, may be a more personal measure of his legacy.

Through the foundation and his work building Legacy Motor Club, Johnson has found ways to keep contributing to the sport and the wider community long after his full-time driving career ended. But this isn't a story about a champion finally learning to sit still. Johnson has made it clear that he remains as competitive as ever, even if the arena has changed.

"The driving force is, I'm not done competing," he said. "I've come to realize that the business space is really damn competitive. And Mr. Hendrick used to always say that to me, if one day when you're not behind the wheel, you'll see how competitive the business side is."

"I'm not done; I'm one that cannot sit still. My purpose bucket, my competitive bucket, those two were really what drove me into this. And then, yes, I can continue my legacy on. I can have this next chapter in this industry. It creates that opportunity, but what's behind it is really purpose and competitiveness."

For Johnson, then, legacy isn't simply what remains after the racing is over. It's what he builds while he's still competing.

This article was originally published on Forbes.com

title: ‘Overdue’ – Dave Portnoy thanks Indiana Fever GM for pointing out ‘insane’ fan bias against the team
description: Dave Portnoy, who has been a staunch supporter of the Indiana Fever because of Caitlin Clark, is tired of the criticism he and other fans have faced. The Fever have become the most polarising WNBA team, partly due to their players and their actions both on and off the court.
fullText:
Dave Portnoy, who has been a staunch supporter of the Indiana Fever because of Caitlin Clark, is tired of the criticism he and other fans have faced.

The Fever have become the most polarising WNBA team, partly due to their players and their actions both on and off the court.

In response to this, the Fever's fanbase has been dubbed one of the most negative in the league, a sentiment GM Amber Cox is not willing to accept.

Indiana Fever GM Amber Cox read out a statement at the team's season-ending press conference in which she decried the media narratives about their franchise's fans.

Seeing this statement, Dave Portnoy, a huge fan of the Indiana Fever, thanked the GM and the front office for delivering a message that he felt had been long overdue.

Portnoy has been one of the most vocal supporters of the Indiana Fever for the last few years, especially since the arrival of Caitlin Clark to the team.

Earlier this season, after Sophie Cunningham's comments on trans athletes in the WNBA, the Indiana Fever began attracting a lot of supporters who align with her sentiments.

This influx of supporters against trans athletes did not sit well with a large portion of longtime WNBA fans, who felt that they were undermining a lot of what the league has represented for years.

On top of that, the overall treatment from fans towards other players, especially those who are rivals of Caitlin Clark's, has earned a lot of scorn from fans of other franchises.

Most recently, there was a controversial incident during Game 2 of the Fever's series with the Las Vegas Aces involving A'ja Wilson.

Wilson got into it with a fan whom she alleged was disrespectful to her, and it became a huge talking point among other fans.

For their part, the Fever reviewed the incident and determined that the fan had not violated the code of conduct, and took no action against him.

title: The Red Sox Wild Card exit was no plot twist
description: It was a predictable epilogue, and the cost of coasting
fullText:
I'm still processing all my feelings over here, and having gone through the Wild Card Series itself already, I find myself back at September's regular-season games. We saw them go 12-12 on the month, as Chad Tracy allowed players to rest and conserve their energy for the postseason. I am starting to see their September fade not just as a slump, but as a trap they collectively bought—or fell—into.

In these days of three Wild Cards, conventional wisdom basically says all you have to do is get in, use your best two or three reliable starting pitchers for this short playoff round, and get hot at the right time. Conventional wisdom also says that anything can happen in the postseason, but the Sox liked their chances, particularly due to the strength of their top three starters. This was a rotation built to handle a three-game sprint, which was consistently mentioned in predictions prior to the series. (This was true even when the edge was actually given to the Yankees; MLB's positional breakdown is one example.)

In fact, speculating about who would pitch the crucial Games 1 and 2 in the Wild Card Series became a main focus in September as fans, the manager, and the team turned their attention to the playoffs. With a postseason berth assured and no real chance to take over the division, the Red Sox paced themselves by resting their starters and other players, to ensure they were ready.

Tracy said about Willson Contreras, ""DH'ing yesterday [instead of playing first base] was strictly to manage the load."

After three losses in a row (to the Guardians and Tampa Bay Rays), he said: "I told the guys before, we earned the right to be in position to be able to line things up."

What Tracy meant is prioritizing rest and conserving energy ahead of the postseason. I hear some entitlement in this and that doesn't sit well with me. They drifted through a completely uninspired September because they "earned the right" to do it that way. Where's the grit? Where's the burning desire to compete and win?

At one point, I remember Lou Merloni saying that the way Tracy handled the roster down the stretch (shuffling lineups, resting players, and experimenting with matchups and platoon roles) reminded him of a spring training evaluation period instead of a September playoff push.

The Sox finished the final month of the regular season with the fewest runs scored in all of Major League Baseball: a measly 71. The team above them, the spiraling Phillies, scored 89. The Brewers scored the most for the month, with 146. I would argue that when the Sox coasted their way through September, they didn't conserve energy—they atrophied.

They "earned the right" to glide their way through September, operating under the delusion that momentum can be toggled on and off at will and that the postseason stage would automatically trigger their best selves. There's that "just get in" mentality.

The Red Sox wrote a hell of a story in 2026. So why didn't they treat the postseason as the action-packed continuation of that page-turner? Instead of continuing to build toward the climax of that story, they slowed down the pace and gave us an anticlimactic month of baseball. Even off the field, in the last week of the regular season, the front office celebrated prematurely when they handed Tracy a three-year deal and picked up both of Craig Breslow's contract options. All before the postseason even began. The timing was odd.

The team spent a month resting on the field, with the really unfortunate result of turning their playoff run into an epilogue—a few extra words tacked onto the end of a story that had already said all it needed to say. When they were outscored 18-2 and swept by the Yankees, it was a heartbreaking ending, for sure, but it wasn't a plot twist. It was the punctuation mark on a sentence they started writing weeks prior.

title: Verstappen wins Bahrain GP in Malaysia after long delays
description: Max Verstappen takes his and Red Bull's first win of the year with a dominant drive in a dramatic Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia that started amid chaotic and unprecedented scenes.
fullText:
Max Verstappen took his and Red Bull's first win of the year with a dominant drive in a dramatic Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia that started amid chaotic and unprecedented scenes.

Verstappen led home the Mercedes of Kimi Antonelli, who took a giant leap towards his first world title when team-mate George Russell retired from third place with a power unit failure with five laps to go.

Antonelli now leads Russell by 84 points with either six or seven races remaining.

Lewis Hamilton drove an extraordinary race after dropping towards the back with an incorrect tyre choice for a wet start to fight back to pass Red Bull's Isack Hadjar for third place with three laps to go.

All that came after a delay of an hour and a half caused initially by heavy rain and then by a series of bizarre technical problems that left several cars crawling as they completed formation laps on the wet track behind the safety car.

After that problem, it took some time for governing body the FIA to decide the order in which the cars should take the start.

The key stories of a madcap afternoon were:

Verstappen's dominant win in a revived Red Bull

The effective death knell for Russell's already faint title hopes

A stunning recovery by Hamilton

A series of questions over race organisation, particularly over the start

Once the race got under way, with the cars in their original order, Verstappen and Hamilton on the front row immediately lost ground and the Mercedes of Antonelli and Russell swept past them into first and second places.

Verstappen and the Mercedes drivers took the start on intermediate tyres on the still-wet track after a torrential tropical downpour had delayed the start.

Hamilton chose soft-compound slicks and immediately regretted the decision as it became apparent that the track was still far too wet for that option. He and others who chose slicks immediately dropped to the back of the field, and lost nearly a minute to the leaders in the early laps.

Meanwhile, Verstappen repassed Russell for second place on lap six, and was on Antonelli's tail when a safety car was deployed to allow marshals to recover the Cadillac of Valtteri Bottas, who had spun off at Turn 13 on lap nine.

The leaders took the opportunity of the safety car to pit for slick tyres, and when the race resumed four laps later, Verstappen immediately passed Antonelli at Turn Four, the Italian also losing out to Russell on the exit of the corner.

From that moment on, Verstappen was total in control and he edged away into a race of his own.

Behind him, Antonelli had pace on Russell and passed him on lap 21 at Turn Four, the move seemingly settling the top three positions.

A late safety car caused by Alex Albon's stricken Williams led to everyone switching to fresh tyres for a four-lap dash to the flag, but again Verstappen was supreme and remained unchallenged.

Even then, there was drama, as Russell pulled off just before Turn One with five laps to go before the safety car had even ended.

In the immediate aftermath, Lando Norris was apparently distracted by Russell's car and had to take to the gravel at Turn One to avoid running into the back of team-mate Oscar Piastri, dropping from eighth to 11th.

He recovered to ninth by the end, immediately behind Fernando Alonso, who scored points for Aston Martin for only the third time this year after their strongest performance of the year.

Hamilton and the others who chose to use dry tyres at the start immediately lived to regret their decision, as they were passed by all the cars on intermediates.

Within a few laps, Hamilton was nearly a minute behind the leaders and down in 17th place, his race apparently over.

But he stayed out during the safety car, sticking with the soft tyres he had chosen for the start, and when the race restarted he began to pick off the cars in front of him, driving an excellent race to get back into contention for serious points.

Hamilton passed car after car until by lap 24 he was on the tail of Isack Hadjar's fourth-placed Red Bull.

They pitted together on lap 31, Hadjar sticking to soft tyres, and Hamilton having no choice but to move to mediums.

Hamilton trailed the Frenchman for lap after lap, right on his tail, but was never quite able to get close enough to pass, despite a number of attempts, before the late safety car.

That gave Hamilton the chance to switch to the preferred soft tyres, and a lap after the restart he passed Hadjar into Turn One to take the final podium position.

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc also passed Hadjar in the closing laps, with Oscar Piastri taking sixth after a dispiriting weekend for McLaren, ahead of Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson and Alonso.

Norris and the second Racing Bulls of Arvid Lindblad completed the top 10.

After the tropical downpour, the race was initially started with formation laps behind the safety car. But immediately the problems stated.

Verstappen and Hamilton were the first of a number of cars that were afflicted by a software issue that left them unable to do more than crawl along.

Initial indications were that this was caused by a software update issued to teams by governing body the FIA during the start delay. The FIA has yet to respond to requests for comment on the matter.

Most teams who were afflicted managed eventually to get their cars going, but the field order was jumbled, and that led to a debate as to the positions in which the cars should take the restart.

The rules did not cover the situation, which was unprecedented. And although they outline positional penalties for any driver who is not able to regain his position by a certain place on the track having lost it on a formation lap, this was ignored in restarting the race in its original order.

title: Ladd McConkey Injury Update: Chargers WR’s Week 4 Status Revealed
description: Ladd McConkey has battled injuries throughout the 2026 season, and while he is officially questionable with a foot injury, he should suit up for Week 4's battle against the Seattle Seahawks. Originally entering the league as a second-round pick in the 2024 NFL Draft, the Georgia product took the league by storm and immeidately established …
fullText:
Ladd McConkey has battled injuries throughout the 2026 season, and while he is officially questionable with a foot injury, he should suit up for Week 4's battle against the Seattle Seahawks. Originally entering the league as a second-round pick in the 2024 NFL Draft, the Georgia product took the league by storm and immeidately established himself as one of Justin Herbert's most reliable targets. Starting in 14 games while making 16 appearances, the wideout finished his inaugural campaign with 82 receptions for 1,149 yards and seven touchdowns on 112 targets. While he wasn't quite as effective in Year 2, he remained a key part of the offense.

Now entering Week 4, Ladd McConkey has been one of the few consistent weapons in the Los Angeles Chargers offense, and he should suit up for a must-win game against the Seattle Seahawks. While nothing is official as of this posting, NFL Network's Ian Rapoport tweeted that the pass-catcher is "likely to play today."

It's hard to overstate just how important Ladd McConkey is for the Chargers to have any shot at pulling an upset against the Seattle Seahawks. While the Los Angeles offense has struggled to reach its ceiling under offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel, McConkey has found a way to record 12 receptions for 183 yards and a touchdown despite playing through a variety of injuries.

It's hard to call any game a "must-win" this early in the season, but that's exactly what Week 4 is for the Los Angeles Chargers. At 0-3, the team is already three games behind the Kansas City Chiefs and Las Vegas Raiders for the AFC West crown, and their Wild Card chances are starting to slip as well. There is basically no presedent for an 0-4 team to make the playoffs, and Ladd McConkey is pretty much the only shot this team has of moving the football. Seattle has one of the league's best defenses, and the Chargers will need their top receiver to play his best football if they want to come out on top.

title: Green Bay Packers to see an undrafted rookie QB’s first NFL start against the Buccaneers
description: The Tampa Bay Buccaneers elevated quarterback Easton Stick and linebacker Caden Fordham from the practice squad Saturday, one day before hosting the Green Bay Packers in Week 4. Stick will back up rookie Jalon Daniels, who is set to make his NFL starting debut in place of Baker Mayfield. Mayfield dislocated his right thumb late [...]
fullText:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers elevated quarterback Easton Stick and linebacker Caden Fordham from the practice squad Saturday, one day before hosting the Green Bay Packers in Week 4.

Stick will back up rookie Jalon Daniels, who is set to make his NFL starting debut in place of Baker Mayfield. Mayfield dislocated his right thumb late in Tampa Bay's Week 3 loss to the Minnesota Vikings, and the Buccaneers said he is expected to miss at least three weeks.

It will snap Mayfield's streak of 57 consecutive starts for Tampa Bay, including the postseason, according to the Buccaneers.

The Packers come to Tampa at 1-2 after a rough outing in Atlanta, where they lost 35-14 on Sept. 24. Tampa Bay is still searching for its first win at 0-3.

Daniels signed with the Buccaneers as an undrafted free agent in May after six seasons at Kansas. Sports Illustrated reported that Tampa Bay named him Mayfield's backup on Aug. 30, the same weekend it released Jake Browning in final cuts.

Sunday will make him the first undrafted rookie to start a regular-season game at quarterback for the Buccaneers, according to the team.

Daniels appeared in 49 games at Kansas from 2020 to 2025. He completed 734 of 1,193 passes for 9,282 yards and 67 touchdowns. On the ground, he added 1,445 yards and 23 more scores.

Tampa Bay signed Stick to its practice squad Aug. 31. He already has some familiarity with offensive coordinator Zac Robinson's system after spending last season with Robinson in Atlanta.

The Los Angeles Chargers selected Stick in the fifth round of the 2019 NFL Draft. He has appeared in six NFL games and started four of them, completing 111 of 174 passes for 1,129 yards, three touchdowns and one interception.

This is the first practice-squad elevation of the season for both Stick and Fordham. Players can be elevated up to three times during the regular season before a team would need to sign them to the active roster to use them again. Stick and Fordham will automatically return to the practice squad after Sunday's game without going through waivers.

Fordham signed with Tampa Bay as an undrafted rookie in May and made the initial 53-man roster after cuts Aug. 30. Three days later, the Buccaneers waived him to make room for cornerback Kevin Knowles, a waiver claim from Kansas City, and brought Fordham back on the practice squad.

At North Carolina State, Fordham made 143 tackles in 2025, second in the nation. He also made his mark on special teams during the preseason, leading all NFL players with four solo tackles in kick coverage.

That could put Fordham directly into the mix Sunday. Linebacker SirVocea Dennis is questionable with a calf injury, and Buccaneers.com noted that Fordham is likely to see work in the kicking game, particularly if Dennis is unavailable.

Green Bay also adjusted its roster Saturday, placing defensive tackle Warren Brinson on injured reserve while linebacker Edgerrin Cooper cleared the concussion protocol [INTERNAL LINK: WISH Brinson IR / Cooper story, once live]. Cooper had opened the week as a limited participant because of the concussion on Green Bay's first injury report.

title: Alvini plays down Frosinone’s flying start: ‘Survival is the only objective’
description: Massimiliano Alvini is refusing to let Frosinone’s excellent opening weeks shift the target, insisting survival remains the only objective.Speaking at the Festival dello Sport in Trento, the coach w...
fullText:
Massimiliano Alvini is refusing to let Frosinone's excellent opening weeks shift the target, insisting survival remains the only objective.

Speaking at the Festival dello Sport in Trento, the coach was asked whether his side had crept up on people.

"We have a single objective, as the president said today, and it's achieving safety. It'll be difficult, it'll be a very long journey," Alvini said, with quotes via TuttoMercatoWeb.

"Now we restart on Saturday. At this moment we've been on an important journey but we're aware of what awaits us. We're not looking now at whether we've done well."

He made clear what would constitute success. "The nicest result is if you then achieve survival at the end of the journey. You have to enjoy that."

FROSINONE, ITALY – SEPTEMBER 06: Antonio Raimondo of Frosinone Calcio celebrates after scoring goal 2-0 during the Serie A match between Frosinone Calcio and Venezia FC at Stadio Benito Stirpe on September 06, 2026 in Frosinone, Italy. (Photo by Giuseppe Bellini/Getty Images)

Antonio Raimondo's availability for the trip to Napoli is uncertain after the forward was released from the Italy Under-21 camp.

"I don't know. We'll see, he's having treatment. We'll see mid-week."

Raimondo has four goals already, a tally bettered only by Donyell Malen, and Juventus are reportedly monitoring him as part of a revamped scouting approach. Giorgi Kvernadze, who Roma are tracking at a €25m valuation, has been similarly productive on the other flank.

ITALY – SEPTEMBER 06: Antonio Raimondo of Frosinone Calcio celebrates after scoring opening goal during the Serie A match at Stadio Benito Stirpe on September 06, 2026 in Frosinone, Italy. (Photo by Giuseppe Bellini/Getty Images)

Alvini confirmed that Bobcek could yet partner Raimondo. "Yes. Bobcek arrived in the last days of the window and needed to get himself into condition a bit. He's ready. We're very happy with him and with the signing. He'll give us a hand."

He also batted away a question about his players and Euro 2028. "You see those things. I have to think about coaching them and improving them."

fullText:
Neighbours say crowds drawn by TikTok to Fabel Friet are clogging the picturesque canal street and attracting litter, gulls and rats

People living in one of Amsterdam’s most exclusive neighbourhoods have taken the city to court for licensing a chip shop that has gone viral on TikTok.

On busy days, the queue for Fabel Friet on Runstraat stretches across a bridge on the Keizersgracht – one of Amsterdam’s most famous canals – a court was told last week. The narrow street itself is crowded by tourists waiting for their orders seven days a week. And loitering with intent – on parked cars, on the street itself, and on steps and porches – gulls wait to swoop.

“We are in a kind of war where a very unwelcome chip shop has polluted the whole area,” said Thomas van Leeuwen, who lives nearby. “Eating in the street is a shameful behaviour. It gets filthy food on our doorsteps and mayonnaise in the beautiful stone. The herring gulls have moved in as residents, and the worst thing is the rat infestation.”

Nineteen neighbours have formally protested against the business licence for Fabel Friet, whose signature product is fries topped with parmesan cheese and truffle mayonnaise. Niek van der Heijden, the lead plaintiff, said the problem was the takeaway’s small size.

“What we call the ‘TikTok queue’ for Fabel Friet causes the most nuisance,” he said. “The business takes place on the street: waiting to order, waiting to be served, eating. We want Fabel to go to a place where there is enough room to have clients inside.”

In a packed courtroom on Tuesday morning, a lawyer for Amsterdam city council acknowledged that the city’s mayor, Femke Halsema, can refuse a licence to operate if the “residential and living environment” is negatively affected by a business.

While the chip shop, she said, sticks to its licence obligations to manage the queue and clear litter “it has been going on for a long time, the impact remains severe, and you have to ask: how long can we tolerate this?” For the current licence, she said, the city would be guided by the court’s ruling.

The shop’s owners, Abel Klatser and Floris Feilzer, said they employed a cleaning service seven days a week, four times a day, and that year-on-year visitor numbers had dropped by 23% this August after they opened four new locations. “A few neighbours have experienced nuisance, but other people enjoy eating chips,” said Gertjan Teeuwen, their lawyer. “It can be busy, but there are peaks and troughs.”

Klatser and Feilzer said in a public statement that they felt unfairly attacked while doing their best to be good neighbours. “Fabel Friet is our child, and we have put our heart and soul into it,” they said. “It is painful if people talk about our business negatively.”

The case goes beyond irritations about so-called performative tourism, where tourists flock to a place to post images on social media. “The tiny streets might be charming, but actually the space is not designed for so many people,” said Lisa-Bobbie Kamp, a lawyer for the neighbours. “This is a question of taking space, who owns the place and whether you can just use public space.”

Marije Peute, a PhD student at the University of Amsterdam, has studied the effects of “viral urbanism” in the neighbourhood. “The municipality should really think about how they want to act, because this is about the public space. A lot of much older retail spaces have lost their local clients because they don’t want to go there any more,” she said.

Rogier Havelaar, a councillor from the Christian Democratic Appeal party, said that, while Fabel Friet should probably be offered a “flagship store” licence in a more suitable location, the benefits of tourism to the city should not be overlooked. “Amsterdam would never have as many museums, restaurants, going-out spots and theatres if they were only for the residents,” he said. “And tourism provides 70,000 jobs. Amsterdam would have a gigantic financial problem if tourism went away.”

Standing on the bridge over the Keizersgracht, some German laboratory apprentices drawn by TikTok were enjoying their chips. Natalie Stübben said crowd managers had just asked them to move away from people’s houses. “It’s pretty hard to get through here with a car or just by walking,” she said. “I don’t think we were thinking about annoying the neighbours, but it makes sense.”

Some of those neighbours will be pleased if the business location has had its chips after the court verdict on 12 November. “There’s something very alarming about the fact that these people are all led by their higher power – influencers – and call themselves followers,” said van Leeuwen. “It’s Orwellian. This court case is part of the parasitic industry that lives on tourists.”

fullText:
Tennessee officials are still investigating why death row inmate Christa Pike survived an execution attempt after receiving two doses of pentobarbital, a drug intended to render a person unconscious and ultimately cause death.

While the immediate focus has been on what went wrong inside the execution chamber, experts say Pike's case has also renewed scrutiny of a problem that has been building for more than a decade: how states obtain lethal injection drugs after pharmaceutical companies moved aggressively to keep their products from being used in executions. Despite those efforts, pentobarbital remains the primary execution drug used by many death-penalty states, making questions about sourcing, testing and oversight especially significant.

The issue has reshaped how many states carry out executions, forcing them to change drug protocols, seek alternative suppliers and adopt increasingly secretive procurement practices.

"Drug shortages have devastated this country's execution process to an unparalleled degree," Deborah Denno, a Fordham University law professor who has studied lethal injection for decades, told Newsweek on Saturday.

For years, states relied on commercially manufactured drugs obtained through traditional pharmaceutical channels.

That began to change after major drug manufacturers objected to having medicines designed to treat patients used in executions.

According to Corinna Barrett Lain, a University of Richmond law professor and author of Secrets of the Killing State: The Untold Story of Lethal Injection, pharmaceutical companies have spent years trying to prevent their products from reaching execution chambers.

"The bottom line is these drug companies, from the start, did not want their drugs being used in lethal injections with executions," Lain told Newsweek on Saturday.

Drugmakers increasingly adopted distribution controls and contractual restrictions barring execution use. The result, according to Lain, is that states seeking lethal injection drugs are now forced to look elsewhere.

"Now states trying to buy drugs for lethal injection are stuck either intentionally breaching private contracts, and getting sued when they are discovered doing so, or buying compounded drugs from whatever compounding pharmacy is willing to sell a sterile injectable barbiturate without a prescription for cash in an under-the-table transaction," she said.

As pharmaceutical companies tightened restrictions, states increasingly turned to alternative methods of obtaining execution drugs.

Some relied on compounding pharmacies, which create customized formulations of drugs rather than mass-produced pharmaceutical products. Others sought alternative suppliers or adopted increasingly secretive procurement practices.

Lain said those shifts have fundamentally changed the execution-drug market.

Joel Zivot, a professor at Emory University School of Medicine, said the restrictions imposed by drug manufacturers forced states to seek alternative sources of execution drugs.

"A gray market usually means legal goods moving through channels the manufacturer never authorized," he told Newsweek on Saturday. "None of the pathways states now use to obtain execution drugs is a white market. Some fit the gray description. Others have crossed into unlawful territory."

Asked whether the term "gray market" accurately describes the current system, Lain replied: "Gray market and black market. Absolutely."

Federal authorities have previously blocked or seized imported execution drugs intended for several states, while courts have reviewed disputes involving overseas suppliers and execution-drug imports.

The problem, according to experts, is that secrecy makes it difficult to know exactly how states obtain many of the drugs they use.

States generally argue that supplier secrecy is necessary because manufacturers and vendors could face public pressure, boycotts or litigation if their identities become public.

Critics say secrecy serves another purpose.

"States can't fix what's broken with lethal injection, and if you can't fix it, the other option is to hide it," Lain said. "It is actually easier for states to fight over secrecy than to reveal the indefensible details of the suppliers they've used."

Zivot likewise argued that secrecy itself has become central to the system.

"Secrecy makes independent evaluation impossible, and that is its purpose," he said.

Without public information about suppliers, storage methods and testing procedures, outside experts cannot independently evaluate the quality or reliability of execution drugs, he said.

"Without knowing who made a drug, how it was stored and whether it was tested, no one, including the courts, can judge whether it will work as the state claims," Zivot said.

Denno said secrecy has steadily expanded over the past two decades.

"The secrecy prevents a systematic analysis," she said. "Yet, all of my research suggests these efforts to get drugs are more opaque and unconventional than ever."

In conventional medicine, intravenous drugs undergo extensive testing and quality-control reviews. Potency, sterility, stability and contamination levels are all subject to regulatory scrutiny.

Questions about execution drugs extend beyond where they come from.

Execution drugs often operate under a different system.

"The question uses the language of medicine, and these chemicals are not medicine," Zivot said. "They are intended as poisons, which turns the usual safety questions upside down."

The distinction matters, he said.

With medicine, regulators worry a drug may be too potent. In an execution setting, a drug that is weaker than expected may fail to kill.

"Because sourcing, storage and testing are kept secret, no one outside the process can say what standards, if any, apply," Zivot said. "That uncertainty is itself the problem."

Tennessee has faced similar questions before. In 2022, Governor Bill Lee paused executions and ordered an independent review after officials discovered the state had failed to follow its own lethal injection procedures. The review later found that drugs prepared for executions had not consistently received all required testing, prompting Tennessee to revise its protocols before executions resumed in 2025.

Yet the state's handling of execution drugs has remained under scrutiny.

Lain said she was unaware of another modern case in which an inmate appeared to survive after lethal-injection drugs had actually been administered. Based on publicly reported evidence, she said IV infiltration appears the most likely explanation, meaning the pentobarbital may have entered surrounding tissue rather than the bloodstream.

Pike's attorneys have similarly argued that execution personnel failed to recognize that IV lines were improperly placed or that veins had blown during the procedure. Tennessee's official review remains ongoing.

Regardless of the ultimate findings, both Lain and Zivot say the episode highlights broader vulnerabilities in the lethal-injection process.

"The death row population is a geriatric population with histories of poor health and often IV drug use," Lain said. "This is a demographic with notoriously weak veins. That's a problem inherent to lethal injection. You're not going to be able to fix that."

Zivot pointed to similar concerns.

"The execution team must place and maintain an IV line in a person who may have difficult veins," he said. "And there is no medical plan for when things go wrong."

Despite the attention surrounding Pike's case, experts disagree about whether it will lead to major reform.

Denno noted that execution failures have repeatedly generated public outrage only for states to continue using lethal injection afterward.

"Unfortunately, yes," she said when asked whether states can continue relying on lethal injection despite mounting procurement problems. "Lethal injection botches are a never-ending story in the United States."

States may continue searching for drugs, altering protocols and defending secrecy measures, she said.

But the underlying problem is unlikely to disappear.

Tennessee's investigation may ultimately determine what happened in Pike's execution attempt. But experts say the episode has also highlighted a separate question: whether states can continue relying on drugs that have become increasingly difficult to obtain, test and scrutinize.

Denno argued that a system originally intended to make executions appear more clinical and humane is now confronting a fundamental contradiction: It depends on drugs that the companies producing them increasingly do not want associated with executions.

title: U.S. Marine detained in connection to woman's 'brutal' death in Japan
description:

Shinjiro Koizumi, the Japanese minister of defense, said a U.S.
fullText:
Officials in Japan said they lodged a "strong" protest with the United States.

A U.S. service member was arrested on suspicion of murder and robbery after a Japanese woman's body was discovered in a hotel in Okinawa, local officials said, describing the alleged killing as a "heinous" incident that prompted the Japanese government to lodge a protest with the United States.

Shinjiro Koizumi, the Japanese minister of defense, said a U.S. Marine lance corporal was arrested on Sunday after the woman's body was found early on Saturday in Naha, the capital city of the Okinawa prefecture.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the Okinawa Prefectural Police were investigating the incident as a murder.

"The occurrence of such an extremely brutal and heinous incident is a matter of profound regret, and as the Government of Japan, we have lodged a strong protest with the U.S. side," she said on social media.

NHK, Japan's public broadcaster, identified the suspect as Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who was stationed at U.S. Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, a base a few miles outside Naha. The broadcaster identified the alleged victim as Yagi Anna, 39, saying she was pronounced dead at the scene.

U.S. officials did not immediately confirm the identity of the service member who was arrested, nor did they say whether the person had been officially charged in connection with the death.

"We are actively cooperating with Japanese authorities, in response to allegations of serious criminal actions by a Marine assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force," the force said in a statement on social media. "We extend our deepest condolences to the victim’s family and friends."

Tens of thousands of U.S. troops are stationed across Japan, including in the country's southernmost prefecture, Okinawa, which is home to several U.S. bases.

The U.S. Embassy in Tokyo said it was aware of the incident and was extending "our deepest condolences to the bereaved family of the deceased."

"At present, an investigation is underway to clarify the facts, and the United States Government continues to cooperate closely with the Government of Japan and local authorities," the embassy said in a statement.

George Glass, the U.S. ambassador to Japan, said he had spoken on Sunday morning with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Okinawa's governor, adding that his office was providing full cooperation with an investigation into the death.

title: Cornell president says university will examine role of Greek life after rape allegation
description:
Cornell University
As outrage builds around the case involving a Cornell University student allegedly gang-raped in a fraternity house in October 2024, the university’s president has broken his silence with a statement Saturday.
Here’s the latest:
University president speaks out: “This is a defining moment in Cornell’s history,” Cornell’s president, Michael Kotlikoff, said in the video statement calling Jane Doe’s allegations “deeply disturbing.” Kotlikoff said he supports the governor’s decision to turn the criminal investigation over to the New York Attorney General and welcomes an independent review by an outside law firm into Cornell’s handling of the 2024 case, which he said Cornell’s board would announce next week. He acknowledged the university does not have all the answers and must “do better” to prevent future sexual violence in the community.
DA declined additional evidence: The Tompkins County District Attorney’s Office in November 2024 declined to review any additional evidence, including more interviews gathered by the campus police department beyond the six-page statement signed by accuser Jane Doe, records obtained by the New York Times show.
fullText:
As outrage builds around the case involving a Cornell University student allegedly gang-raped in a fraternity house in October 2024, the university’s president has broken his silence with a statement Saturday.

Jane Doe’s alleged experiences raise “heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization, and aspects of party culture, alcohol, and drug use,” Kotlikoff said in his video statement.

The Cornell president added the allegations raise questions around the initial investigation, saying the university does not have “all the answers” but is committed to investigating and finding them. He said next week, Cornell’s board of trustees will announce an independent review into the handling of the 2024 case by an outside law firm.

While Cornell had released a statement after Doe filed her lawsuit in September and later launched an FAQ page on the allegations, Saturday’s remarks from Kotlikoff mark his first on-camera statement on the case.

Kotlikoff said he backs legislative efforts to change New York’s sexual assault law and Hochul’s decision to appoint a special prosecutor in the investigation – a move the university previously told CNN it supported.

While the criminal investigation and review are underway, the university will work to strengthen programs surrounding sexual assault prevention and education, mental health and substance use, he added.

Addressing frustrations surrounding Cornell’s communications about the case, he said “we will make a greater effort to explain what we can, to provide context about the actions Cornell has taken, and to be more transparent” within the confines of legal and policy limits.

Toward the end of his statement, Kotlikoff signaled support for reviewing the role of Greek organizations in campus life. “We will reengage students, alumni, and other members of our community to examine how we preserve what is valuable about Greek life while strengthening individual accountability, transparency, and a culture in which every member understands their responsibility to protect the safety and well-being of others,” he said.

Doe’s attorney, Thomas Giuffra, said he is hopeful but wary about the promises Kotlikoff made. “We are hopeful that his statement is backed up by meaningful reforms that leads to real change for the sake of the students at Cornell,” he told CNN in a statement Saturday.

Snapchat messages, a Cornell disciplinary panel’s decision, a cache of documents from the university’s formal Title IX investigation obtained by The New York Times and phone recordings by Jane Doe reviewed by ABC News have shed new light on what may have happened in the fraternity house. The sources also help clarify Doe’s reported frame of mind at points on the night that began October 19, 2024, and how her understanding of the events changed as she processed her trauma in the following weeks.

When Doe first went to campus police, authorities documented that she reported “she was recently raped by 8-10 men at the Chi Phi fraternity house,” according to documents reviewed by ABC News. CNN has asked campus police for a copy of the report.

The phrase does not appear in the six-page statement sent to prosecutors.

Cornell is facing scrutiny because the university initially said campus police investigated the allegations in 2024 and “shared all investigatory information with the Tompkins County District Attorney’s Office.” But the school later changed its statement, now saying police investigated the allegations in 2024 and “shared the victim’s sworn statement and the Snapchat screenshot” with the DA’s office.

Van Houten previously said his office did not bring criminal charges because of Doe’s six-page statement. He later said his office had access to some Snapchat messages exchanged during the alleged assault in a group chat titled, “Chi Phi Actives.” Images of one Snapchat chain obtained by CNN include a photo of Doe in a room at the fraternity house during the time she describes being assaulted.

Doe also made an explicit allegation of rape in her interview that was not included in the six-page statement furnished to prosecutors, according to WCBS. Although Doe did recount being hit and feeling emotionally coerced in the statement, it did not include some stronger language or allegations she used in her interview, according to The New York Times, citing documents it obtained.

Among the documents obtained by the Times also were records showing the district attorney’s office declined to review any additional evidence gathered by the campus police department beyond the six-page statement signed by Doe. A Cornell police investigator spoke to a member of the district attorney’s staff on November 25, 2024, about reviewing additional evidence, the Times said. By that time, university police had conducted more interviews and reviewed chat messages, the Times report said.

But prosecutors did not express interest in the additional evidence because they had decided that, based on Doe’s statement, “Criminal charges would not be pursued in this case,” a Cornell police investigator said in a note documenting the call. When reached for comment, the district attorney staff member referred all questions to the district attorney, the Times reported.

Van Houten told the Times by email that any additional records gathered by the Cornell police were “not pertinent to our analysis because we had Jane Doe’s comprehensive account of the events.” CNN reached out to Van Houten’s office for comment Friday.

CNN obtained a copy of a heavily redacted, 99-page document summarizing key evidence included in a Cornell disciplinary panel’s decision, which supports the Times’ findings about how Doe later came to understand the night’s events as assault. The panel’s decision details more than 50 interviews, including with six of the seven accused men.

Additionally, Jane Doe three weeks after the incident asked the fraternity member who invited her to the house that night, “Do you remember how any of these guys walked in?” her phone recordings reviewed by ABC News indicate.

He made no mention of his group chat invitation, ABC News reported, instead explaining to Doe, “The door was just unlocked. … The party was sort of like crowded. … There was nowhere else to go.”

Doe told him, “If I wanted to take this somewhere, what y’all did would be classified as gang rape,” she told him, ABC News reported, noting Doe’s recorded phone calls to at least three of the fraternity brothers were later turned over to university investigators.

One of the men Doe has accused of sexual assault reportedly sent her this text message: “I just wanted to apologize for how things went down the other night,” according to records obtained by The New York Times and corroborated by Doe’s attorney. The sender said he and another male allegedly involved felt terrible and too under the influence of drugs and alcohol to “shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand.”

“I’m so sorry,” another alleged attacker told Doe around the same time in a message ABC News reviewed. “I feel so bad for you, dude.”

The initial university investigation led to suspensions and expulsions for the accused students, according to Doe’s attorney, the barring of the fraternity chapter from campus and the launch of a sexual assault task force. Four of the Chi Phi fraternity members acknowledged having sexual contact with Doe but said their interactions had been consensual. The others denied participating in sexual encounters, the Times reported.

Amid the renewed investigation, court documents show a Chi Phi fraternity member named as a defendant in Doe’s civil suit has been petitioning New York state courts to invalidate a university disciplinary decision that found him responsible for attempted sexual exploitation.

Help is available: For help in the US, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673 or chat 24/7 on online.rainn.org.

CNN’s Rebekah Riess, Holly Yan, Jessie Yeung, Gloria Pazmino, Jason Carroll, Alisha Ebrahimji, Jake Tapper and Mark Morales contributed to this report.

Marquez wins in Japan to cut Martin's MotoGP lead
description: Defending MotoGP champion Marc Marquez wins a sprint-race double at the Japanese Grand Prix to cut Jorge Martin's championship lead to two points.
fullText:
Reigning MotoGP champion Marc Marquez took maximum points at the Japanese Grand Prix, winning Saturday's sprint and Sunday's race, to cut fellow Spaniard Jorge Martin's championship lead to just two points.

Martin, 28, who won the title in 2024, finished second after starting Sunday's race at Motegi Circuit in pole position, while his Aprilla team-mate Marco Bezzecchi was third.

Ducati rider Marquez, 33, had to bide his time after Martin held his advantage off the line, but the seven-time champion took his chance on the 11th lap to edge past his rival on the inside.

"The race was tough, especially when I was behind Jorge, but I knew that if I was able to lead the race, my pace was good," said Marquez, who moved to 331 points with six rounds remaining.

"Jorge tried to attack, but then I just increased a bit more the pace and it was enough to do the last two laps more relaxed."

Italian Bezzecchi, 27, moved to 284 points to keep his slim title hopes alive after fending off a late charge by Tech3's Enea Bastianini to claim his place on the podium.

Gresini's Alex Marquez had a race to forget, crashing out after serving a double long lap penalty for his role in a three-rider collision during Saturday's sprint.

title: Burgess ready to stay on to end Warrington pain
description: Sam Burgess says he plans to stay at Warrington for 2027 as the Wolves try to bounce back from more Grand Final heartache.
fullText:
Warrington Wolves head coach Sam Burgess confirmed he is going to stay with the club for next year as the dust settles on yet another near miss in the Grand Final.

Saturday's 23-10 loss to Wakefield Trinity means Warrington have been losing finalists five times on Super League's biggest stage.

But having led the Wolves back to Old Trafford for the first time since 2018, Burgess - whose side also suffered narrow Challenge Cup final defeats in 2024 and 2025 - wants the pain to drive them on.

The 37-year-old is yet to agree terms for 2027 and beyond, but he has offered reassurances to the club's owner Simon Moran about his future.

"I've not signed a contract yet but I've given my word to Simon Moran and that's probably better than any contract," said Burgess.

"I truly believe in where we're going as a club and the identity we've created. In the middle of the season, we had 15 players injured and the academy system held us together.

"It'll be the same again next year and I truly believe in our philosophy."

Wakefield beat Warrington to win Super League

'An unbelievable story' - inside unfancied Wakefield's rapid ascent

Quiz: Name every Super League Grand Finalist

That philosophy was characterised by the appearances of scrum-half Ewan Irwin and centre Arron Lindop at Old Trafford.

Irwin is still only 18 and Lindop just two years older - but they contributed all 10 of their side's points against Wakefield with Lindop crossing for both tries and Irwin adding a conversion.

It is the emergence of that duo and others who are waiting in the wings that gives Burgess belief there will not be another eight-year wait to return to the domestic game's biggest stage.

"This is more of a beginning," said the man who won the National Rugby League Premiership in Australia with South Sydney Rabbitohs in 2014.

"We've understood what it takes to get here now - well certainly I have - and the squad we are building now is getting more towards 'my' squad.

"We've understood as a club and a staff what it takes to get here and we're determined to take that next step, but we have got to keep improving.

"I guess we have to let the pain of today drive us forward tomorrow."

For now, that leaves Warrington as the nearly men of rugby league with Wakefield, and not the Wire, becoming the sixth club to join the elite band of Super League winners.

title: 'New queen' Silva beats Wang to UFC flyweight title
description: Natalia Silva is crowned the new women's flyweight champion with a unanimous decision victory over China's Wang Cong at UFC 332.
fullText:
Natalia Silva was crowned the new women's UFC flyweight champion as she claimed the vacant title with a unanimous decision victory over China's Wang Cong at UFC 332.

Silva had been set to face Kyrgyzstan's Valentina Shevchenko for the title before their bout was cancelled, with Shevchenko forced to vacate the belt last month because of injury.

But the Brazilian extended her winning streak to 15 bouts with a dominant victory against Wang over five rounds in Salt Lake City.

"I want to tell this to everyone... don't give up on anything," Silva said in her post-fight interview.

"This belt here is because God gave me the opportunity. I knew [Wang] was a tough fighter. This fight proved why she was challenging me.

"This is the beginning of Natalia Silva. I'm the new queen."

The 29-year-old, who entered the bout as favourite, led the judges' scorecards with tallies of 48-47, 48-47 and 49-46.

Shevchenko later congratulated Silva on social media and warned her not to get "too comfortable".

"Well deserved Natalia! Congratulations," Shevchenko wrote on X.

"It's my pleasure to know that UFC Champion's belt is now holding deserving martial artist - such as you are.

"But don't get too comfortable - keep it warm, I'm coming soon for my belt."

It was the first women's main event in the UFC since Mackenzie Dern beat Amanda Ribas in January 2025, while it was the first time two women headlined one of the UFC's flagship numbered events since June 2023, when Amanda Nunes defeated Irene Aldana.

Earlier, Britain's Mick Parkin lasted less than four minutes in the octagon as he was knocked out by a knee from Johnny Walker on the Brazilian's heavyweight debut.

title: Wales aiming to prove they can thrive at top level
description: Captain Ben Davies says Wales will be driven by determination to prove they can live with challenges of Nations League A when they face Denmark in Cardiff.
fullText:
Captain Ben Davies says Wales will be driven by a determination to prove they can thrive in Nations League A when they face Denmark in Cardiff on Sunday.

Wales go into the game in buoyant mood after ending a six-game winless sequence by taking the scalp of Norway on Thursday.

But having registered Wales' first ever victory in the Nations League's top tier, Craig Bellamy's players are hungry for more.

"We don't want to be in a situation where you feel like you're not competing against bigger teams," said defender Davies.

"But I thought we laid a good marker down the other night [against Norway] to show that we do belong playing against these teams - it was a much better all-round performance.

"I think we really got back to what's got us to success and got us into the Nations League A in the first place. Hopefully we can replicate that [against Denmark]."

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC Two Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru and 5 Live, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

Wales came from behind against Norway to secure a 2-1 success which eased the pressure built during their run without a win, which stretched back to the thrashing of North Macedonia last November.

Defeat against Bosnia-Herzegovina in the World Cup play-off semi-final came next, before friendly draws against Northern Ireland and Ghana were followed by successive defeats to Romania, Portugal and the Danes.

That left Bellamy and his players in need of a result as they met Norway, and they responded by delivering a rousing display.

Wales' cause was helped by Norway defender Torbjorn Heggem's red card early in the second half, but they had troubled the World Cup quarter-finalists even before the sending off.

"The teams at this level are all strong," added 103-cap Tottenham defender Davies.

"All the games are going to be tough but we're here to compete and here to try to give the best account of us that we can.

"I thought we did that the other night and it was really pleasing to get the three points. It gives us, as a group, a lot of confidence going into the games coming up."

Group has 'exploded' after Wales win - Bellamy

Why beating Denmark matters to Wales' Euro 2028 hopes

Wales will again be without the likes of Karl Darlow, Joe Rodon, Dylan Lawlor, David Brooks and Harry Wilson because of injury as they look to maintain the momentum gained thanks to the Norway triumph.

Bellamy says he has no choice but to make changes to the side which began on Thursday as Wales seek to make amends for last Sunday's defeat in Denmark.

Having emerged with some credit despite losing their Nations League opener against Portugal 10 days ago, Wales were well beaten on a demoralising evening in Copenhagen.

Davies hopes the Cardiff City Stadium factor will be key as Wales chase victory against a Danish side who, in 21st, are 17 places above them in the Fifa rankings.

"It does make a big difference going away. We didn't get a grip on the game [in Denmark] whereas when we played Norway in Cardiff, it's our home, our fans, our atmosphere," he said.

"It felt like a different game and we had much more control… you just know you have to try to make your home advantage count."

title: I clawed my way to the top but need a break - Azpilicueta
description: Cesar Azpilicueta says it is time to move to "a different stage of life" following a glorious 20-year playing career, notably captaining Chelsea to several titles.
fullText:
Cesar Azpilicueta was an all-encompassing leader for Chelsea - and, now retired, he reflects on how his passion for education and attention to detail helped him build a career at the highest level.

One story sums it up. Before Chelsea's Champions League final victory in 2021, Azpilicueta could not take his customary pre-match nap and opted to study instead.

He says his work towards an MBA in business management from the Berlin School of Business and Innovation took his mind off the pressure and noise on the streets of Porto.

Later that day, he lifted the Champions League trophy after captaining Chelsea to victory against Manchester City.

Azpilicueta told BBC Sport: "When I was a kid my parents pushed me to get good grades and finish school.

"I wasn't a professional footballer until I was 17, in my last year of school. Education was always important. When Covid-19 arrived, we had more time.

"I found some courses but I didn't start because I thought it was the end of my career. It was more that I wanted to learn, improve myself and do it in another language.

"It wasn't because I thought it was my last year as a footballer, but it did help me navigate the final years of my career, become a better person and a better footballer."

Azpilicueta, 37, was speaking at Arsenal's Emirates Stadium, where he joked he did not feel "entirely comfortable", while collecting a diploma in global football sport directorship through the PFA Business School, adding to qualifications that also include a diploma from Harvard Business School.

Now retired from playing after spending last season at Sevilla, he replied "maybe" when asked whether he could become a sporting director one day, but says football has left him in need of a post-career break.

Now at a "different stage of life", he cannot even contemplate playing football with friends for fun because it would trigger his competitive instincts.

"It was time to stop playing football because, even though I could probably still play, I didn't have the energy to commit myself fully for an entire season," he reflected.

"At the moment I have another commitment, which is my family. I want to play some golf and enjoy life.

"For 20 years I was constantly travelling, playing and preparing for seasons. This summer looked completely different."

After beginning at boyhood club Osasuna, Azpilicueta joined Marseille, where he learned French. However, it was his move to Chelsea in 2012 that proved transformative.

Completing his latest course highlights Azpilicueta's thirst for knowledge and a desire for constant self-improvement.

It was something he learned at Chelsea, where he arrived as a relatively low-profile £7m signing in a dressing room full of established leaders such as John Terry, Frank Lampard and Petr Cech, alongside star names including Fernando Torres, Eden Hazard and Ashley Cole.

He explained: "I started as a right winger, moved to France, then moved to Chelsea. I wasn't a star signing. I had to find my way. Left-back, wing-back, centre-back in a back three.

"It was about consistency. I had to work hard to stay fit, adapt to different managers and different positions.

"When you arrive at Chelsea, you feel the ambition straight away. Every three days you have to win. Every game and every trophy matters.

"That culture pushed me to the maximum and, especially when I left Chelsea, I felt that I had given everything I had for the club."

Azpilicueta explained how his education away from the pitch helped him develop into a leader at Stamford Bridge.

It gave him the confidence to represent Premier League players during the Covid-19 pandemic, while also helping to organise initiatives and keep the club moving forward after owner Roman Abramovich was sanctioned following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

His defining moment came in that 2021 Champions League final victory.

There is little doubt that, having succeeded Terry and then Gary Cahill as captain, Azpilicueta ranks among Chelsea's greatest leaders. Yet he revealed that, since leaving the club in 2023, he has not returned to Stamford Bridge.

He was among dozens of players to leave after Chelsea changed ownership from Abramovich to the current American-led consortium in 2022.

"I left Chelsea, but Chelsea will always stay in my heart," he said. "I follow every game and I hope the club comes back to where it belongs.

"There are some very strong teams around and football sometimes needs a bit of time. You need connections, people playing together and understanding each other.

"At a big club like Chelsea, the demands are high. But I think that's normal. It should be demanding and ambitious because, speaking as a Chelsea fan, you always want to see the club winning trophies.

"I have confidence that [manager] Xabi [Alonso], the staff and the players will do good work. Hopefully they can bring a lot of happiness to the fans."

He has been following Chelsea's latest captain Reece James, who he believes will grow into a better leader, since over-30 players Jordan Henderson, Danny Welbeck and Emiliano Martinez joined over the summer.

When it is suggested that he might return to Stamford Bridge in some capacity to be marked by a warm reception from supporters, Azpilicueta responds modestly: "I don't know about that.

"I will come back one day. I won't be putting on my boots, though."
